issues.body:
# `function_call_output` for `send_message_to_thread` is persisted without `call_id`, breaking any strict Responses API provider

## Summary

Rollout records for **async cross-thread tool results** (`send_message_to_thread`, namespace
`codex_app`) are written as `function_call_output` items **without a `call_id` field**.

OpenAI's own backend tolerates the malformed item. Any provider that strictly deserializes the
Responses API `input` array rejects the **entire request**:

```
Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: input: missing field `call_id`
```

Because the bad record stays in thread history, the thread becomes permanently unusable on such
providers once that record falls inside the retained context window.

## Environment

- Codex app (bundled codex): `0.154.0-alpha.6.2`
  (`/Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/codex`)
- Codex CLI: `0.147.0`
- macOS (Darwin 25.6.0), Apple silicon
- Provider: custom `[model_providers.*]` entry pointing at an OpenAI-compatible
  `/responses` endpoint

## Observed record

Taken from a rollout at `~/.codex/sessions/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/*.jsonl`:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-09-16T...",
  "type": "response_item",
  "payload": {
    "type": "function_call_output",
    "id": "fco_01a06a8e-65c1-7e22-8b84-c42ca9cf1b6c",
    "name": "send_message_to_thread",
    "namespace": "codex_app",
    "output": "<codex_delegation>...</codex_delegation>"
  }
}
```

`call_id` is absent. In the same thread, the corresponding **calls** are well-formed:

```
function_call         send_message_to_thread   16 items  — all carry call_id
function_call_output  send_message_to_thread    6 items  — none carry call_id
```

Positionally, these outputs appear at the **start of a later turn** (immediately following a
`turn_context` entry) — i.e. they are the async result of a delegation issued in a previous turn.

## Scale and date range

Four long-lived threads in one workspace:

| thread | bad records | first occurrence |
|---|---:|---|
| A | 284 | 2026-08-31 01:33:52 |
| B | 164 | 2026-08-31 08:57:50 |
| C | 221 | 2026-09-08 07:53:04 |
| D |  84 | 2026-09-04 03:55:12 |

- Tool attribution in thread A: **281 / 284** are `send_message_to_thread` (3 have no `name`).
- Month distribution in thread A (thread created 2026-07-18):
  `2026-07: 0`, `2026-08: 7`, `2026-09: 277`.

**Two independent threads both first show the defect on 2026-08-31**, which should bracket the
regression window.

## Minimal reproduction (API level)

Verified 2026-09-16 against a strict OpenAI-compatible `/responses` implementation:

```
POST {base_url}/responses
{
  "model": "...",
  "input": [
    {"type": "message", "role": "user",
     "content": [{"type": "input_text", "text": "hi"}]},
    {"type": "function_call_output", "id": "fco_test", "output": "test"}
  ]
}
→ 400 {"error":{"message":"Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type:
                   input: missing field `call_id`", ...}}
```

Supplying an arbitrary `call_id` does **not** help either:

```
→ 400 {"error":{"message":"No tool call found for tool output with call_id call_test", ...}}
```

So the fix must produce an output that is **paired with a real call**, not merely populated.

## Expected behaviour

Every `function_call_output` written to a rollout should carry the `call_id` of its originating
call. For async results whose originating call is no longer in the retained history, either
re-emit the call or drop the orphan output when constructing the Responses `input` array.

## Impact

- Once a bad record enters the retained window, the thread fails on every turn and cannot be
  recovered without manual mutation of the rollout files.
- The async-result path keeps firing, so **new bad records accumulate continuously** — the
  problem grows with use rather than being a one-off.
- Users cannot tell which threads are affected until they hit the error; the failure looks like a
  provider fault rather than a history-corruption fault.

## Additional notes

- A codex-side log line exists: `Orphan function call output for call id: …`, so orphan handling
  is present — it just does not cover the *missing field* case, which is what breaks strict
  deserializers.
- Happy to provide redacted rollout excerpts or a script that counts affected records in a
  `CODEX_HOME` if that would help.

## Why

Codex checks candidate Bubblewrap executables before sandbox confinement.

prs.title: Honor declared filesystem permissions in Windows sandboxes
prs.body:
Honor declared filesystem permissions in Windows sandboxes

## Why

MXC volume expansion can generate child grants that override restrictions on
directory aliases. The restricted-token backend can also reject valid workspace
policies because its compatibility check assumes the working directory is
writable.

## What changed

- Check directory identity before MXC expands writable volume roots. Suppress
  generated write grants that conflict with read-only aliases, including through
  junctions on other volumes, while preserving narrower explicit grants.
  Reject launch if a writable volume is also denied or its relationship to a
  restricted directory cannot be determined.
- Let the restricted-token backend accept the supplied workspace roots when
  the working directory has no explicit write grant, while retaining exact
  root matching for filesystem-root write grants.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for restricted volume aliases, junctions across
writable roots, explicit drive-root denials, and restricted-token workspace
roots with nested or read-only working directories or an empty root list.

prs.title: Preserve Linux sandbox restrictions across writable symlink aliases
prs.body:
Preserve Linux sandbox restrictions across writable symlink aliases

## Why

Ordering writable binds by the spelled paths can put a parent mount
after a child mount when symlinks are involved. The later bind can cover
deny masks and read-only mounts that the sandbox already applied.

## What changed

Group writable roots by their resolved mount destinations and bind each
destination once, with parents before descendants. Map deny rules under
writable aliases to their physical paths and apply them after read-only
mounts. Reapply read-only mounts below each writable bind while
preserving explicit write grants for narrower paths.

## Testing

Add `bwrap` regression cases for a symlink to `/` paired with a project
alias and for aliases to nested project directories. The cases check
that denied files stay unreadable, read-only files resist writes, and
explicitly writable children remain usable under restricted parents.

Seal synthetic mounts in read-restricted Linux sandboxes

## Why

Read-restricted sandboxes build a synthetic filesystem around paths
granted by policy. Leaving the backing mounts writable lets commands
modify synthetic directories outside explicitly writable paths.

## What changed

Remount the synthetic root, minimal `/dev`, and applicable WSL masks
read-only after bubblewrap finishes setting up mounts. The remounts
are nonrecursive, so explicitly writable child mounts stay writable.

## Testing

Extend the sandbox regression test to check that commands can read an
approved file through a symlink, write to `/dev/null`, and write to an
allowed subdirectory under a denied parent. The test also checks that
commands cannot rename the synthetic directory containing the approved
file or create an ungranted directory under `/dev`.

prs.body:
Show confirmed thread permissions in TUI status

## Why

The TUI used its local configuration to report permissions and approvals.
Pending profile selections could make those values differ from the
settings confirmed for the displayed thread. Legacy sandbox policies
can also hide restrictions of named profiles.

## What changed

- Use the displayed thread's confirmed permissions and approval settings
  in `/status`, the built-in status line, and status line provider data.
  Show unknown values in the UI when the thread has no confirmed settings.
- For named custom profiles, show the profile name and approval mode in

## What happened?

The [Skills management table in the CLI reference](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/60f8082b14ffa7f10b608270232f3f57b5abbec8/docs/cli/cli-reference.md#L121-L134) lists `gemini skills enable --all` and `gemini skills disable --all` as bulk commands. ## Steps to reproduce

From a source checkout of `60f8082b14ffa7f10b608270232f3f57b5abbec8`, install dependencies and build with `npm ci` and `npm run build`, then run:

```sh
npm start -- skills enable --all

```

The first two commands exit 1 with `Not enough non-option arguments: got 0, need at least 1`. The third command's help describes `--all` as including built-in skills in the list.

The CLI reference should show `gemini skills enable <name>` and `gemini skills disable <name>` for changing an individual skill, and `gemini skills list --all` for listing skills including built-ins.

Reproduced from source on macOS arm64 using Node.js 20.19.5. These CLI invocations do not require account login.

labels.name: priority/p2

labels.name: area/agent

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

### What happened?

This is purely anecdotal, but IME Gemini does not use custom skills and sub-agents on its own, basically at all.  It will if I instruct it to explicitly, but won't when it's doing something very related.

For example, I have "gradle" and "git" skills with descriptions like:
> Executes and manages Gradle builds authoritatively with high-performance background orchestration 
  and surgical failure analysis. This skill is the STRONGLY PREFERRED way 
  to run any Gradle task, providing superior reliability through managed background processes, 
  task-specific output capturing, and deep diagnostic integration. Use it for executing core 
  lifecycle tasks like 'build' or 'assemble', starting persistent development servers, 
  or performing complex build troubleshooting. Do NOT use for specialized test diagnostics 
  (use running_gradle_tests).

and 
> Audits Git repository status, examines history, and implements non-interactive modifications. Processes surgical staging, descriptive commits, and multi-file diff analysis. Use for repository introspection and history-based truth verification. NEVER stages or commits without explicit user directives. Avoids interactive prompts via --no-pager.

that never ever get called when using the relevant tools.

I even have this in my `GEMINI.md` in the "priority rules" section:
> 4. **Agent & Tool Hierarchy:** Whenver considering how to approach a task or do anything, ALWAYS follow the hierarchy of preference: **Sub-Agents** > **Skills** > **Specialized MCP Tools** (NOT a Shell tool or similar) > **General/Builtin Tools** (e.g., `run_shell_command`, `grep_search`, `read_file`).
> 5. **Intentionality Protocol:** Before starting ANY task, you MUST stop and consider which agent, skill, or tool is most appropriate for the specific context. If your plan involves using the shell (even via a tool like `run_shell_command`), you MUST stop and reconsider if a more specialized tool or skill exists to handle the task more reliably.

I expected Gemini to use related skills when working on tasks that match the skill description.  Same for sub-agents.

### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

labels.name: priority/p3

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: docs(cli): correct the skills command reference
prs.body:
## Summary

Correct the Skills management table in the CLI reference. The two bulk enable and disable examples fail because both commands require a skill name.

## Details

Keep the existing named enable and disable examples. Document `gemini skills list --all` as the way to include built-in skills in the list, and remove the two invalid examples. This updates the reference to match the CLI's current behavior.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30505

## How to Validate

After building from the repository root, run:

```sh
npm start -- skills enable --help
npm start -- skills disable --help
npm start -- skills list --help
```

prs.title: fix(core): respect active YOLO mode in taint and build file checks
prs.body:
## Summary

Respect active, trusted YOLO mode (`--approval-mode=yolo` / `-y`) in shell taint/build-file risk checks and `PolicyEngine` build file protection so autonomous interactive and headless (`-y -p`) YOLO runs are no longer interrupted by confirmation prompts or hard-denied (`POLICY_VIOLATION`) when editing build configuration files or running commands referencing external context.

All indirect prompt-injection protections remain fully enforced in `default` and `auto_edit` modes, in untrusted folders (`!isTrustedFolder()`), when YOLO mode is administratively disabled (`disableYoloMode` / `secureModeEnabled` / `isYoloModeDisabled()`), when safety checkers (`checkerRunner`) deny/ask, and when higher-tier user/admin policy rules or `BeforeTool` hooks explicitly require `ask_user` or `deny`.

## Details

1. **`PolicyEngine` & `Config` (`packages/core/src/policy/types.ts`, `packages/core/src/policy/policy-engine.ts`, `packages/core/src/config/config.ts`)**:
   - Added optional `isYoloModeDisabled?: () => boolean` to `PolicyEngineConfig` and wired it from `Config` (`isYoloModeDisabled: () => this.isYoloModeDisabled()`), initializing `this.disableYoloMode` prior to `PolicyEngine` construction.
   - Skipped the hardcoded `Build File Protection` downgrade (`ASK_USER` / `DENY` on `package.json`, `Makefile`, `BUILD.bazel`, etc.) only when `this.approvalMode === ApprovalMode.YOLO && this.isTrustedFolder() && !this.isYoloModeDisabled()`.
   - Explicit higher-tier `ASK_USER` / `DENY` policy rules and safety checkers continue to run unchanged.
2. **`ShellToolInvocation` (`packages/core/src/tools/shell.ts`)**:
   - Added `isActiveYoloMode()` verifying `ApprovalMode.YOLO`, `isTrustedFolder() !== false`, and `!isYoloModeDisabled()`.
   - Updated `shouldConfirmExecute()` to skip forcing confirmation for `hasTaintedOrBuildFileRisk()` when active YOLO mode is enabled (unless `forcedDecision === 'ask_user'` from an explicit policy rule or hook).
   - Updated `isCommandSubstitutionAllowed()` so active YOLO mode delegates command substitution checks to `PolicyEngine` (`yolo.toml` sets `allowCommandSubstitution = true`) rather than unconditionally blocking on `hasTaintedOrBuildFileRisk()`.
   - Preserved the `hasTaintedOrBuildFileRisk()` guard in `getPolicyUpdateOptions()` so tainted commands never persist permanent `"Always allow"` rules.
3. **`Scheduler` (`packages/core/src/scheduler/scheduler.ts`)**:
   - Skipped escalating `PolicyDecision.ALLOW` to `ASK_USER` (interactive) or `DENY` (non-interactive/headless) for `hasTaintedOrBuildFileRisk()` only when `ApprovalMode.YOLO`, `isTrustedFolder() !== false`, and `!isYoloModeDisabled()`.

## Security Invariants Preserved

| Context | Taint / Build-File Protection |
|---|---|
| `default` / `auto_edit` / `plan` modes | Enforced (`ASK_USER` / `DENY` in headless) |
| Untrusted folder (`!isTrustedFolder()`) | Enforced even if `approvalMode === YOLO` |
| Admin-disabled YOLO (`disableYoloMode` / `secureModeEnabled`) | Enforced across `PolicyEngine`, `Scheduler`, and `ShellToolInvocation` |
| Explicit higher-tier user/admin `ASK_USER` / `DENY` rules or `BeforeTool` hooks | Enforced in active YOLO mode |
| `"Always allow"` policy persistence for tainted commands | Still blocked (`getPolicyUpdateOptions()` returns `undefined`) |
| Trusted, active `--yolo` / `-y` (interactive & headless `-p`) | Allowed per `yolo.toml` without hardcoded interruption |

*(Open to gating this behind an explicit `security.*` setting if maintainers prefer opt-in over default behavior in trusted YOLO mode.)*

## Related Issues

Fixes #30004
Related: #29682, #29680, #29687

## How to Validate

- Targeted unit tests (`policy-engine.test.ts`, `config.test.ts`, `shell.test.ts`, `scheduler.test.ts`):
  ```bash
  npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/policy/policy-engine.test.ts src/config/config.test.ts src/tools/shell.test.ts src/scheduler/scheduler.test.ts
  ```
  Result: **4 test files passed, 583 tests passed**.
- CLI config/settings/confirmation tests (`config.test.ts`, `settings.test.ts`, `ToolConfirmationMessage.test.tsx`): **3 test files passed, 424 tests passed**.
- A2A server tests (`@google/gemini-cli-a2a-server`): **17 test files passed, 329 tests passed**.
- Workspace build (`npm run build --workspaces`), full monorepo typecheck (`npm run typecheck`), and strict ESLint (`--max-warnings 0`) on all modified files: **all passed with 0 errors/warnings**.

- [x] Rebased cleanly onto latest `main` (`08e9a20`) with no merge conflicts
- [x] Unit tests added/updated for active YOLO, headless YOLO, untrusted folders, `disableYoloMode`, higher-tier policy rules, and `forcedDecision: 'ask_user'`

prs.title: fix(sandbox): improve permission denial detection and unsupported environment handling (#29338)
prs.body:
## Description
Fixes #29338.

This PR addresses sandbox compatibility and permission error handling across containerized and restricted execution environments in `@google/gemini-cli-core`.

### Issues Addressed
1. **Permission Denials Unrecognized**: POSIX sandbox denial detection previously missed common tool-level permission errors (`mkdir: cannot create directory`, `touch: cannot touch`, `chmod: changing permissions of`, `scandir`, `access`, and Python `[Errno 13]`). This prevented the CLI from identifying file permission denials and offering dynamic permission resolution.
2. **Unhandled Crash on Unsupported Environments**: When tool sandboxing was requested in environments without supported sandbox managers, `LocalSandboxManager` threw an untyped generic error rather than the canonical `FatalSandboxError` (exit code 44), causing an unhandled crash rather than graceful user diagnostic exit.

### Changes Made
- `packages/core/src/sandbox/utils/sandboxDenialUtils.ts`:
  - Extended `isFileDenial` keyword detection for `cannot create directory`, `cannot touch`, `changing permissions of`, and `errno 13`.
  - Added dedicated extraction regexes for `mkdir`, `touch`, `chmod`, `scandir`, `access`, Python `[Errno 13]`, and shell permission denied errors.
- `packages/core/src/services/sandboxManager.ts`:
  - Updated `LocalSandboxManager.prepareCommand()` to throw `FatalSandboxError` with actionable remediation guidance.
- `packages/core/src/sandbox/utils/sandboxDenialUtils.test.ts`:
  - Added 8 regression test cases covering all new permission denial formats and `FatalSandboxError` verification.

## How Was This Tested?
- Added regression tests in `sandboxDenialUtils.test.ts` for all permission error formats.
- Verified `LocalSandboxManager` throws `FatalSandboxError` with exit code 44 (`ExitCodes.FATAL_SANDBOX_ERROR`).

prs.body:
## Description
This PR centralizes and unifies CLI process exit codes across `@google/gemini-cli-core`.

Previously, `ExitCodes` in `exitCodes.ts` was missing several fatal error codes that were hardcoded as raw numeric literals in `errors.ts` (`FatalSandboxError`, `FatalTurnLimitedError`, `FatalToolExecutionError`, and `FatalUntrustedWorkspaceError`). Furthermore, `FatalError` subclasses in `errors.ts` used raw magic numbers rather than referencing the canonical `ExitCodes` constant.

This change:
1. Adds the missing fatal exit codes (`44`, `53`, `54`, `55`) to `ExitCodes`.
2. Exports the strongly-typed `ExitCode` union for autocomplete and compile-time validation.
3. Refactors all `FatalError` subclasses to reference `ExitCodes.*`.
4. Adds a comprehensive unit test suite in `exitCodes.test.ts` to ensure 100% test coverage and prevent future regressions.

## Changes Made
- `packages/core/src/utils/exitCodes.ts`:
  - Added `FATAL_SANDBOX_ERROR: 44`
  - Added `FATAL_TURN_LIMITED_ERROR: 53`
  - Added `FATAL_TOOL_EXECUTION_ERROR: 54`
  - Added `FATAL_UNTRUSTED_WORKSPACE_ERROR: 55`
  - Exported `type ExitCode = (typeof ExitCodes)[keyof typeof ExitCodes]`
- `packages/core/src/utils/errors.ts`:
  - Imported `ExitCodes` from `./exitCodes.js`
  - Replaced all magic numbers in `FatalError` subclasses with `ExitCodes.FATAL_*`
- `packages/core/src/utils/exitCodes.test.ts`:

  - Canonical numeric exit code mappings.

prs.title: fix(cli): detect local git clone installation from CLI executable path
prs.body:
## Summary
Fixes an issue where running Gemini CLI from a source checkout outside of the clone directory causes `getInstallationInfo` to misclassify the installation as a global npm install, triggering an unintended background `npm install -g @google/gemini-cli@latest` during auto-update.

Fixes #30209

## Details
In `packages/cli/src/utils/installationInfo.ts`, local git clone detection previously relied on:
```ts
isGitRepository(process.cwd()) &&
realPath.startsWith(normalizedProjectRoot) &&
!realPath.includes('/node_modules/')
```
Because `projectRoot` comes from `config.getProjectRoot()` (which is the current target directory / `process.cwd()`), running the CLI from any other directory caused `realPath.startsWith(normalizedProjectRoot)` or `isGitRepository(process.cwd())` to fail. As a result, detection fell through to the default branch (`PackageManager.NPM`, `isGlobal: true`), spawning `npm install -g` in the background.

This fix:
- Updates the detection to check `!realPath.includes('/node_modules/') && isGitRepository(path.dirname(realPath))`, inspecting where the CLI executable itself is located rather than the user's working directory.
- Preserves the `node_modules` exclusion so package-manager installations (npx, npm, pnpm, yarn, bun) remain unaffected.
- Updates existing tests and adds unit test coverage in `installationInfo.test.ts` for running a local clone from an unrelated working directory.

## Related Issues
Fixes #30209

## How to Validate
Run the unit tests in `packages/cli`:
```bash
npx vitest run src/utils/installationInfo.test.ts --coverage false
```
Expected: All 22 tests pass, including the test asserting that running from an unrelated working directory is correctly identified as a local git clone.

## Pre-Merge Checklist
- [x] Added/updated tests
- [ ] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [x] Windows (npm run)

prs.title: fix(core): preserve trimmed function-call name in history to prevent 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT (#30256)
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes #30256.

When the model produces a function call whose name contains leading or trailing whitespace (e.g. `" update_topic"`), `Turn.handlePendingFunctionCall` trims the name to dispatch tool execution and constructs the `functionResponse` under that trimmed name (`"update_topic"`). However, the in-place mutation of the function call object in history updated `fnCall.id = callId` but omitted updating `fnCall.name = name`.

On subsequent conversational turns, the paired `functionCall` (`" update_topic"`) and `functionResponse` (`"update_topic"`) carried mismatched names under the same `id`, causing the Gemini API to reject the request with `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT`.

This PR ensures `fnCall.name = name` is consistently written alongside `fnCall.id = callId` during function call handling in `Turn` and stream consolidation in `GeminiChat`.

## Details

1. In `packages/core/src/core/turn.ts`:
   - Updated `Turn.handlePendingFunctionCall` to assign `fnCall.name = name` alongside `fnCall.id = callId`.
2. In `packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.ts`:
   - Updated stream processing loops (both context-management enabled and fallback modes) to set `fnCall.name = name`.
3. In `packages/core/src/core/turn.test.ts` & `packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.test.ts`:
   - Added unit tests verifying that padded function call names are trimmed and recorded consistently in history turns.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30256

## How to Validate

Run unit tests in `packages/core`:
```bash
npm test src/core/turn.test.ts src/core/geminiChat.test.ts
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
```
All pass with 0 errors.

- [x] Validated with `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, and `npm run lint`

prs.title: fix(core): normalize CRLF line endings when computing write_file diffs and diffStat
prs.body:
## TLDR

Fixes #30480.

Normalizes `\r\n` to `\n` before computing the confirmation diff, execution result diff, and `getDiffStat` in `packages/core/src/tools/write-file.ts` (matching `edit.ts`), while keeping raw `originalContent` untouched for `detectLineEnding` so CRLF line endings are still preserved on disk.

## Dive Deeper

- **Root cause:** `write_file` read the existing file raw (preserving `\r\n`) and diffed it against LF model content in both `shouldConfirmExecute` and `execute` (`Diff.createPatch` and `getDiffStat`), causing every unchanged line to appear removed and re-added and inflating `+N/-N` telemetry and rewind counts.
- **Fix:** Normalize `\r\n` to `\n` on the inputs passed to `Diff.createPatch` and `getDiffStat` in `packages/core/src/tools/write-file.ts`. Disk write CRLF detection (`detectLineEnding(originalContent)`) and `getDiffContextSnippet` continue to operate on the raw original and final contents.
- **Tests:** Added a regression test in `packages/core/src/tools/write-file.test.ts` verifying that overwriting 1 line of a 5-line CRLF file produces a 1-line approval diff, a 1-line result diff, `model_added_lines: 1` / `model_removed_lines: 1`, and preserves `\r\n` on disk. Confirmed failing on `main` and passing with this fix.

## Reviewer Test Plan

```bash
npx vitest run packages/core/src/tools/write-file.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false
```

- `packages/core/src/tools/write-file.test.ts`: all tests passing
- `prettier --check` & `eslint --max-warnings 0` on modified files: passed

prs.title: fix(core,cli): consistently support GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID fallback
prs.body:
## Summary

Consistently support `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` as a fallback for `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` across core, CLI, and a2a-server (matching the documented behavior in `docs/get-started/authentication.mdx#set-gcp`), improve Vertex AI missing-location error messaging, and surface actionable project-ID guidance on `IneligibleTierError`.

## Details

Although [authentication docs (`#set-gcp`)](https://geminicli.com/docs/get-started/authentication/#set-gcp), `setupUser`, `oauth2`, `createContentGeneratorConfig`, and `retry` already supported `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` as a fallback for `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`, several remaining paths only inspected `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`:

- **Vertex AI validation & client initialization (`packages/cli/src/config/auth.ts`, `packages/core/src/core/contentGenerator.ts`)**:
  - `validateAuthMethod(AuthType.USE_VERTEX_AI)` now accepts `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` as a fallback for `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`.
  - When a Google Cloud project is configured without `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` (and without `GOOGLE_API_KEY`), validation now returns a targeted message instructing the user to also set `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION`.
  - Because `@google/genai` only reads `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` from the environment, `createContentGenerator` now explicitly passes `project` (and `location` when set) to `new GoogleGenAI(...)` when using Vertex AI with `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` alone.
- **Untrusted `.env` loading & Cloud Shell (`packages/cli/src/config/settings.ts`)**:
  - Added `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` to `AUTH_ENV_VAR_WHITELIST` so `.env` files in untrusted workspaces load and sanitize it identically to `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`.
  - Updated `setUpCloudShellEnvironment` to preserve `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID`, avoid shadowing an explicit `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` with `cloudshell-gca`, and respect (and sanitize when untrusted/sandboxed) `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` from `.env`.
- **Ineligible tier guidance (`packages/core/src/code_assist/setup.ts`)**:
  - Added an optional `projectIdHint` parameter to `IneligibleTierError` so `throwIneligibleOrProjectIdError` appends enterprise project-ID guidance (`GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` or `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` + `#set-gcp` link) separated by `\n\n` without mutating `this.ineligibleTiers`.
- **Sandboxes, telemetry, `/about`, sanitization, and a2a-server**:
  - Forwarded `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` in Docker/Podman and LXC sandboxes (`packages/cli/src/utils/sandbox.ts`).
  - Added `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` fallback to direct GCP telemetry export (`packages/core/src/telemetry/sdk.ts`) and `/about` commands (`packages/cli/src/ui/commands/aboutCommand.ts`, `packages/cli/src/acp/commands/about.ts`).
  - Added `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` to `NEVER_ALLOWED_ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLES` (`packages/core/src/services/environmentSanitization.ts`) and aligned `packages/a2a-server` env handling (`src/agent/task.ts`, `src/http/app.ts`).
- **Docs (`docs/get-started/authentication.mdx`, `docs/reference/configuration.md`)**:
  - Fixed the example heading mismatch in `#set-gcp` and documented the `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` fallback in `configuration.md`.

## Related Issues

Related to #13252

## How to Validate

```bash
npm run build
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm run bundle
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- --run \
  src/code_assist/setup.test.ts \
  src/core/contentGenerator.test.ts \
  src/services/environmentSanitization.test.ts \
  src/telemetry/sdk.test.ts
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- --run \
  src/config/auth.test.ts \
  src/config/settings.test.ts \
  src/ui/commands/aboutCommand.test.ts \
  src/utils/sandbox.test.ts \
  src/core/auth.test.ts \
  src/ui/auth/useAuth.test.tsx \
  src/validateNonInterActiveAuth.test.ts
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-a2a-server -- --run \
  src/agent/task.test.ts \
  src/http/app.test.ts \
  src/config/rce_vulnerability.test.ts
```

Manual edge cases covered by unit tests:
1. Vertex AI auth with `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` + `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` (passes validation and forwards `project`/`location` to `GoogleGenAI`).
2. Vertex AI auth with `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` or `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` set without `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` (surfaces targeted `GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION` error).
3. Untrusted `.env` and Cloud Shell handling of `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID` (sanitized when untrusted, not shadowed by `cloudshell-gca`).
4. `IneligibleTierError` appends enterprise project-ID hint cleanly while leaving `ineligibleTiers` intact.

prs.title: fix(cli): preserve history and stop replay when checkpoint restore fails
prs.body:
## Summary

Preserve the current UI and model history when checkpoint restoration fails, and stop the CLI from replaying the checkpoint's tool after a reported restore error.

## Details

`performRestore` now completes the requested Git restore before yielding `load_history`. Missing Git services, missing trees, and unexpected Git errors leave conversation history intact. Successful restores retain the existing history/message action order, and history-only checkpoints still work.

The CLI stops processing a restore after displaying an error action, before it can return the tool for replay.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30495.

## How to Validate

- Baseline: the regression checks fail on the original code (4 core failures and 3 CLI failures).
- With the fix: all 25 focused tests pass:
  - `npx vitest run --root packages/core --coverage.enabled=false src/commands/restore.test.ts`
  - `npx vitest run --root packages/cli --coverage.enabled=false src/ui/commands/restoreCommand.test.ts`
- `npm run preflight` passed formatting, build, lint, type checks, the CLI suite (8,067 tests), and the other workspace suites. Its initial core run hit five existing native-keychain assertions because it inherited WSL detection variables.
- With `WSL_DISTRO_NAME`, `WSLENV`, and `WSL_INTEROP` unset for the test process, the complete core rerun passed: 9,129 tests. No source changes were needed for that environment adjustment.
- `npm run test:scripts`: 202 passed; `npm run test:sea-launch`: 17 passed.
