prs.title: fix: open the dashboard in a compatible installed browser
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Onboarding and `openclaw dashboard` can open a browser that cannot run the Control UI even when a compatible browser is already installed. Switching browsers using only the clean dashboard URL loses the one-time pairing handoff and creates avoidable recovery work; this is not a failure of normal pairing.

## User Impact

When the default browser is known to lack required features, OpenClaw can open an identified compatible alternative on macOS, native Windows, or Linux for this session only. Supported and unknown defaults keep their existing opening path. No browser is installed, no OS default is changed, and no automation browser profile is selected.

**Native proof pending: macOS fallback from an unsupported HTML default and Windows fresh-profile cold pairing.** Normal macOS dashboard pairing, native Linux fallback and pairing, and guided macOS onboarding with the acknowledgment fix have been reported. Windows Hub is independently released and is not changed here. WSL keeps its existing Windows desktop opener rather than selecting a Linux browser.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing browser opener now accepts an installed-browser target, while the existing private-file handoff still carries each newly issued one-time pairing URL. Browser-version estimates and actual browser feature probes share the same requirements; browser-side verification remains authoritative.

- macOS resolves the default HTML-document handler through Launch Services and reads application registrations/metadata, including `~/Applications`.
- Native Windows queries the Shell for the effective HTML-file handler and reads installed executable versions without running browsers to identify their versions.
- Linux reads the XDG `text/html` association and normal Chrome/Chromium, Firefox, and Edge executables on `PATH`. Custom wrappers, Flatpak-only installations, and `BROWSER` overrides remain conservative unknown cases.
- Selection order is deterministic. Unknown metadata retains the existing fallback, while missing compatible alternatives retain a terminal/recovery path.
- Explicit remote sessions do not launch on the wrong desktop. Cold GUI processes acknowledge startup without waiting for their lifetime; onboarding separately waits for a newly connected Control UI client.

There is no new pairing mechanism, stored browser preference, configuration option, token handling, or installation step. Changes target main only; no backport or older-Gateway compatibility is proposed. Necessary growth is the three platform discovery adapters and their common selection contract; no registry/cache/manager is introduced.

## Evidence

### Guided onboarding acknowledgment and native follow-up

Integrated the [onboarding fix](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c2a1498284d15eb69f66de91d0cfdba96c6cc438) and [test allocation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2951b914a376f86f48dbe4d8f7abe0c05ac78dfc) from the [patch and proof submitted by @oshaughnessy-junior](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200840#issuecomment-7148057153). The published commits have the same trees as the two submitted commits.

- The local onboarding probe requests operator.read for this presence call only. The default session-scoped projection omits the connection fields the wizard needs; server-side redaction, method classification, and authorization ceilings are unchanged.
- The report records one red-to-green regression using the real scope resolver and presence projector, 17 passing handoff tests, 19 passing guided/QuickStart consumer tests, and a native guided macOS/Ollama replay that acknowledged a newly authenticated Control UI connection and exited 0. The replay ran on the submitted behavioral commit; the follow-up only changes the allocation. It did not prove a first chat reply or capture screenshots.
- The scoped allocation is 137 above the standard 400 (537 net test lines on the submitted branch): 5 for the macOS handler regression plus 31 for the onboarding projection regression on top of the existing 101. This preserves distinct platform and private-handoff coverage without changing the global budget. Hosted CI on the updated PR head is separate.
- [Sally’s earlier native report](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200840#issuecomment-7143225573) covers macOS Safari discovery and normal dashboard pairing, plus Linux fallback and pairing with different HTML/HTTPS defaults. Outstanding: macOS fallback from an unsupported HTML default and Windows fresh-profile cold launch with actual pairing.

### Maintainer CI follow-up

Commit: [`a2766a306c97`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/a2766a306c97ac74dfc7948185024c52029434c8).

The selector and platform adapters now import their discovery contract from a types-only module. Browser selection, launch, and pairing behavior are unchanged.

- The static import-cycle guard went from one cycle to zero; the runtime import-cycle guard also passed.
- Consolidated 35 net test lines. The test-line ratchet passes at 501/501: the standard 400 lines plus a scoped 101-line allocation for the distinct OS association, remote/headless, and private-handoff regressions. The global budget is unchanged.
- 98 focused tests across 8 files passed locally in 57.21 seconds for the suite; the edited selector suite was rerun after a lint-only fixture cleanup. Core and scoped test typechecks, targeted lint/format, and diff checks passed. The structured local review runner was unavailable; scoped source review was manual.
- This is not native desktop proof. Current-head macOS verification and Windows fresh-profile cold launch/pairing remain pending.

### Native Windows retest and visible-launch / HTML-association follow-up

Follow-up commit: [`1e5e0cb0a861`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/1e5e0cb0a8618ceec47fd2c591bace46e41cc946). Independent source review found no concrete P0/P1/P2 issue in this follow-up; native execution remains unverified.

[@ekinnee’s retest](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200840#issuecomment-6993850519) of `6f75e6e45291` on Windows 11 26H2 confirms **correct selection**, unchanged HTML/HTTPS associations, protected handoff ACLs, credential-free browser arguments, and **60 passing Windows tests, 1 skipped, 0 failed**. Windows assigned HTML to Chrome 124 and HTTPS to Edge 157; the repaired selector correctly chose Chrome 158. With Chrome already visible in a prepared disposable profile, the dashboard opened and established one fresh authenticated Control UI connection.

**Fresh-profile cold launch/pairing still failed:** the selected process remained alive without a visible main window and admitted no Control UI connection, including a repeat launch. A separate harmless-HTML probe showed a window with `windowsHide: false`, but did not show the probe page title. That isolates a visibility problem, not a complete cold-pairing fix.

The follow-up sets `windowsHide: false` only for directly launched user GUI browsers, retaining detached startup acknowledgement and private-file delivery. It does not add first-run bypass flags, change profiles, or equate a process launch with connection/pairing success.

It also addresses ClawSweeper's HTML-handler finding on macOS/Linux: Launch Services resolves `public.html` with the default role, and XDG resolves `text/html`, matching the file actually passed to the opener instead of an unrelated HTTPS association. Unknown HTML handlers retain the existing opening path. Windows already uses the effective HTML association.

- Six visibility/split-association regressions failed before this follow-up and pass afterward. The Mac regression executes the actual JXA discovery program against fixed native-boundary responses; Linux uses real subprocess fixtures with deliberately different HTML/HTTPS defaults. Neither is native GUI proof.
- **102 focused tests across 8 files pass** (17.68 seconds wall time), plus strict affected typechecking, targeted lint/format, and diff checks.
- **Current-head native verification remains pending**, especially fresh-profile Windows visibility and actual handoff redemption. Prepared-profile success on the earlier head must not be reported as a cold-start pass.

### Windows repair after native verification

Repair commit: [`6f75e6e45291`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/6f75e6e45291e2769e58df887aabf5fd9cde31c1). Independent source review found no concrete P0/P1/P2 findings in this repair; this was not native Windows execution.

[@ekinnee’s native Windows report](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200840#issuecomment-6987294781) exposed a real failure on `cee9b3506c21`: Windows 11 26H2 resolved Chrome 124 as the effective HTTPS/HTML handler, but the legacy `UserChoice` key still named Edge. The PR therefore skipped fallback and opened the unsupported browser, with no admitted Control UI connection. The same run found that the selector suite called POSIX-only `process.getuid()` during shared setup on Windows.

The repair removes legacy default-registration/ProgID command parsing and asks the Windows Shell's `AssocQueryStringW` API for the effective `.html` executable. This is the association used for the private `handoff.html` file; it can differ from HTTPS. Unknown Shell results remain unknown, never fall back to stale default-registration data. Existing application metadata still supplies versions and deterministically ordered alternatives; no browser settings, registrations, installations, or profiles are modified.

Selector fixtures now supply and restore a synthetic macOS UID independently of the native host. Private-file tests run on their real host platform, retaining POSIX permissions versus Windows ACL behavior instead of performing real file operations under a mocked macOS platform.

- Three effective-handler regressions failed before the repair and pass afterward, including unsupported effective Chrome with stale Edge data, a supported effective handler, and an unknown association.
- **100 focused tests across 8 files pass** (16.59 seconds wall time), plus strict affected typechecking, targeted lint/format, and diff checks.
- All **27 selector cases also pass with `process.getuid` removed before the test runner starts** (39.97 seconds wall time, including compilation). This is Linux-hosted portability proof, not native Windows execution.
- **Superseded by the native retest above:** selection, the Windows selector suite, and prepared-profile pairing passed on this repair head; fresh-profile cold launch/pairing did not.

### ClawSweeper repair: inherited SSH variables on macOS

Commit [`cee9b3506c21`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/cee9b3506c218358154da01c7de7bb7ac8afaf75) restores the local-shell behavior protected by [#67088](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/67088) and [#85340](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/85340). SSH environment variables alone no longer reject a local Mac GUI terminal. After verifying the console owner, SSH-marked Mac sessions must identify as the current launchd `Aqua` GUI bootstrap; background, unknown, or failed context checks remain blocked, as do Remote Containers/Codespaces. Linux/Windows SSH and WSL handling are unchanged.

Four inherited-SSH regressions failed on the previous PR head and pass with this repair. **70 focused tests across four affected/consumer files pass** (15.44 seconds wall time), along with strict affected typechecking, targeted lint/format, and diff checks. Independent source review found no concrete P0/P1/P2 issue in this narrow repair. This is fixture/source proof, not a new native macOS run: the earlier report's simulated-SSH result applies to `29dae7868b21`, not the new GUI-context distinction.

### Native macOS dashboard validation — passed

[@jjjhenriksen’s native test report](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200840#issuecomment-6966181964) validates head `29dae7868b2139b5829806475c52b1f9076d2138` against comparison build `e9561fb93e23aca2a797ed0cf28593cac45edc17` in a disposable Apple Silicon Tart VM running macOS Sequoia 15.7.7, using a foreground loopback Gateway and disposable state.

- **Before:** the dashboard opened the HTTPS default, Safari 18.6, which displayed the unsupported-browser screen; the Gateway recorded no admitted Control UI connection.
- **After:** with Safari still the HTTPS default, the dashboard selected Chrome 158.0.8127.37 installed only in `~/Applications`. Both a cold launch and a repeat launch into the running Chrome process produced fresh, authenticated Control UI connections at the Gateway. The HTTPS default remained Safari.
- **Additional checks:** removing the compatible alternative produced the recovery notice; `--no-open` suppressed launch; `--json` returned the handoff and expiry fields; a simulated SSH session suppressed GUI launch.
- **Onboarding is partial, not passed:** the browser-handoff helper selected Chrome and the Gateway recorded a separate fresh Control UI connection, but the helper did not return before the test cutoff. This was not a full interactive onboarding run or confirmed handoff completion.

The report includes sanitized terminal/Gateway excerpts, not before/after screenshots. It does **not** establish supported-default behavior, unknown/custom metadata, failed browser startup, a forced expired handoff, or a successful chat reply.

### Automated and source validation

- **Prior-head validation:** 89 targeted tests across 8 files passed on `29dae7868b21` (16.96 seconds wall time). The repair reruns the four affected/consumer suites above; unchanged feature-floor, private-handoff, Linux subprocess, and browser feature-admission proof is retained from that run. Focused tests cover browser feature floors, supported/unknown defaults, user-installed macOS alternatives, deterministic selection, native Windows metadata fixtures, Linux XDG subprocess fixtures, headless/SSH/WSL behavior, selected-launch failure, cold long-lived GUI process startup, private-file delivery, and fresh handoffs on repeated dashboard runs. Existing dashboard/onboarding handoff suites and browser feature admission remain green.
- Selected-launch regressions were red on base `e9561fb93e23aca2a797ed0cf28593cac45edc17` (three intended failures) and green with the target-aware opener.
- Strict typechecking of affected production/tests with repository ambient declarations, targeted lint/format, and `git diff --check` pass.
- `pnpm ui:build` succeeds. Existing advisory size budgets also fail on the pinned base: CSS 57.8 KiB vs 56.9 KiB; chat boot requests 21 vs 20; chat JS 1297.2 KiB vs 1296.8 KiB. The candidate reports 1297.3 KiB chat JS; no CSS/request-budget exception is added.
- Independent read-only source review identified cold-GUI lifetime and kernel-only WSL classification defects; both were repaired with regressions. The follow-up review confirms both repairs with no remaining concrete P0/P1/P2 findings in those repairs. Native platform execution is not established by that review. The structured Auto Review attempts were interrupted by Gateway restarts and did not produce a completed receipt.

Linux-specific proof uses real Linux subprocesses for XDG discovery fixtures and a real long-lived process for cold-launch lifetime; those pass locally. This runner has no installed desktop browser or display, so real Linux desktop opening/pairing and screenshots remain unverified, not claimed as passing.

### Remaining native verification

Use disposable state/profile and a foreground Gateway on an unused port, never normal Gateway credentials.

- The guided macOS onboarding replay above addresses the prior acknowledgment failure. A separately observed chat reply was not included.
- Verify the new macOS distinction between a local GUI shell carrying inherited SSH variables and an actual SSH/background session belonging to the same console user. Also cover the supported-default and unknown/custom browser paths, failed browser startup, forced expired-handoff recovery, and a separately observed chat reply.
- Rerun fresh-profile Windows cold launch with the visible GUI setting, observe any browser first-run UI, and verify the private handoff actually redeems and admits a new Control UI connection. Repeat with a prepared visible profile and preserve the HTML/HTTPS defaults.
- Verify the new macOS/Linux HTML-handler discovery with differing HTML and HTTPS defaults, including an unknown/custom HTML application. Linux subprocess fixtures and the Mac native-boundary fixture do not establish desktop browser behavior.
- Capture sanitized unsupported-default before/after media with actual OS/browser versions. Do not publish pairing URLs, credentials, or private desktop content.

Reported and scoped with @jjjhenriksen. Native test-box verification is still pending.

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

prs.title: fix(agents): keep bundle MCP access for turns woken by an exec completion
prs.body:
Closes #183589

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: when a backgrounded host exec exits and `tools.exec.notifyOnExit` (default `true`) wakes the originating session, the woken turn has no bundle MCP tools although the run that started the exec had them (Code Mode telemetry `sources: {openclaw: 51, mcp: 0}`, `tools.effective` notice `mcp-not-yet-connected`), and any child spawned from that woken turn inherits the restriction.

## User Impact

User impact: a turn woken by an exec completion keeps exactly the MCP access of the run that started the exec, and children it spawns do too: an unrestricted run keeps every configured server, a run capped to `fixture__*` wakes a turn that can reach only the `fixture` server, an exact-name policy such as `fixture__read` keeps only that tool. Runs with no `mcp.servers`, or whose cap excludes bundle MCP tools, behave exactly as before, so a woken turn never gains access the producer run did not have. No config, schema, or wire change; `notifyOnExit` no longer has to be disabled to keep MCP in long-lived sessions.

## Why This Change Was Made

`createOpenClawCodingTools` (assembled in `src/agents/agent-tools.assembly.ts`) builds each tool's Gateway caller with a default `sessionEventSourcePolicy` whose `toolsAllow` lists the finalized coding tools. Bundle MCP tools are materialized afterwards (`attempt-bundle-tools.ts`), so no `server__tool` name or `bundle-mcp` marker is ever in that list. The exec tool records the policy as the completion event's `producerPolicy`; `captureSessionEventTarget` intersects the woken turn's `toolsAllow` with it; `shouldCreateBundleMcpRuntimeForAttempt` then finds no bundle name and creates no MCP runtime for the woken turn or its children.

The fix captures the producer's final surface instead of predicting it (revision 5). `createOpenClawCodingTools` now fills a caller-owned array (`sessionEventToolsAllowRef`) with the coding tool names and hands that same array to every Gateway caller as `sessionEventSourcePolicy.toolsAllow`. The embedded attempt (`attempt-bundle-tools.ts`) appends the bundled MCP/LSP tools that survived the attempt's runtime allowlist, `applyFinalEffectiveToolPolicy`, and schema projection, by exact name, in the same place it already captures the cron creator cap and the spawn allowlist. The exec tool reads the policy when it records the completion, so the woken turn gets exactly the tools this run could call:

- sender-scoped denials (`tools.toolsBySender["id:alice"].deny: ["admin__*"]`) already removed `admin__reset` from the producer's final surface, so the senderless woken turn never sees it;
- intersected caps, partial globs (`fixture__read*` ∩ `fixture__*All`), and namespace-reaching globs (`fixture*`) are resolved by the existing runtime matcher on real tools, not approximated;
- a refresh replaces the previously appended bundled names, so a tool quarantined or filtered on refresh drops out;
- no marker or glob is ever added, so the continuation cannot widen past the producer.

The surface stays under the existing 512-name bound the target reader enforces (`SESSION_EVENT_TOOLS_ALLOW_LIMIT`, now exported from `session-event-target.ts`); past it, the attempt logs a warning and the woken turn keeps only the coding tools. Revision 5 deletes `agent-tools.session-event-policy.ts` and its tests (revisions 1–4 projected MCP access from allow patterns, which the review showed cannot preserve denials or every glob shape).

## Evidence

Regression in `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-bundle-tools.test.ts` (`session event tool surface`, 9 cases through `prepareEmbeddedAttemptBundleTools` with `fixture` and `admin` servers materializing `fixture__read`, `fixture__readAll`, `fixture__write`, `admin__reset`; each captured cap is then run through the woken turn's `intersectSessionEventToolsAllow` → `shouldCreateBundleMcpRuntimeForAttempt` → `applyEmbeddedAttemptToolsAllow`):

- unrestricted producer → all four MCP tools; `["exec", "fixture__*"]` and `["exec", "fixture*"]` → the three fixture tools; `["exec", "fixture__read"]` → `fixture__read`;
- intersected `[["exec", "fixture__read*"], ["exec", "fixture__*All"]]` → `fixture__readAll` (revision 4 returned nothing here);
- `["read", "exec"]` → no MCP tool and no bundle runtime in the woken turn;
- producer final policy drops `admin__reset` (the sender-scoped denial shape) → the woken turn never admits it;
- refresh after a projection drops `fixture__readAll` → the cap shrinks to `["exec", "fixture__read"]`;
- a coding surface at the bound → MCP names are not appended.

Red on `main`: the attempt never appends to the cap, so every case expecting an MCP tool fails, the reported loss.

Suites: `attempt-bundle-tools` 23/23; `bash-tools.exec-notify`, `tools/gateway-caller-context`, `agent-tools.prefix-stability`, `attempt-tool-prepare.web-search`, `session-event-handoff`, `session-event-context`, `session-event-permissions` 115/115. Oxlint clean; `git diff --check` clean.

### Live Gateway run (revision 5, head 18721460f1e, shipped entry point, scripted provider)

Built dist from this head (`build-all gatewayWatch` with `OPENCLAW_BUILD_PRIVATE_QA=1`), isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, non-interactive onboarding with `--custom-no-auth` against a loopback OpenAI-compatible provider written for the proof. The provider scripts each step from the conversation and logs every request's offered `tools[].function.name`.
Two loopback streamable-http MCP servers, `fixture` (`echo`) and `admin` (`reset`), each log every JSON-RPC request. Config: `mcp.servers` for both, `tools.profile: full`, `tools.codeMode: false`, `tools.toolSearch: false`, `tools.exec.security: full`, `tools.exec.ask: off`, `tools.exec.notifyOnExit: true`; Gateway `node openclaw.mjs gateway run --port 18399`.
Every scenario's producer turn runs `exec` with `background: true` and ends. Its woken turn then calls `fixture__echo`, `sessions_spawn` (child task: `fixture__echo`, then `admin__reset`) and `admin__reset`. The provider emits each call whether or not it was offered, so the Gateway has to refuse what the turn may not use.
Policy changes were applied with `node openclaw.mjs config patch --file …` while the Gateway was running (log: `config hot reload applied (…)`). Times are UTC; tool results come from the session transcript in the agent SQLite store.
No credentials, all loopback; the host was heavily loaded, which explains the minutes between exec exit and wake.

**S1: allowed completion-turn MCP call** (`tools.allow: ["read","exec","process","sessions_spawn","fixture__*"]`, session `agent:main:s3d`, dispatched with `node openclaw.mjs agent --agent main --session-key s3d --json`)

```text
18:40:53.533  provider  producer   offered=exec,fixture__echo,process,read,sessions_spawn,skills_read   -> exec {"command":"sleep 5; echo PROOF_EXEC_DONE","background":true}
18:40:53.686  provider  producer   -> "started" (turn ends, exec still running)
18:56:00.145  provider  woken      last user msg "[OpenClaw exec completion] Exec completed (… code 0) :: PROOF_EXEC_DONE"
                                   offered=exec,fixture__echo,process,read,sessions_spawn,skills_read   -> fixture__echo {"text":"from-woken-turn"}
18:56:00.155  fixture   tools/call echo {"text":"from-woken-turn"}
18:56:00.158  toolResult fixture__echo  "fixture.echo ok: {\"text\":\"from-woken-turn\"}"
18:56:00.279  toolResult admin__reset   isError "Tool admin__reset not found"
admin server: initialize / tools/list only, no tools/call
```

The turn woken by the exec exit got `fixture__echo` and its call reached the fixture server; `admin__reset`, outside the producer's cap, was not offered and was refused before any request left the Gateway.

**S2: sender-scoped admin denial preserved** (no `tools.allow`; `tools.toolsBySender: {"id:alice": {"deny": ["admin__*"]}}`). The producer message entered through the **qa-channel** plugin: the repo's qa-lab bus ran on loopback and `POST /v1/inbound/message` carried `{"conversation":{"id":"alice","kind":"direct"},"senderId":"alice"}`. The producer request shows `"sender":{"id":"alice","name":"Alice"}`.

```text
19:30:58.826  provider  producer (sender alice)  tools=70  fixture__echo=yes  admin__reset=no   -> exec background
19:31:06.503  provider  woken (senderless)       tools=70  fixture__echo=yes  admin__reset=no   -> fixture__echo
19:31:06.598  fixture   tools/call echo {"text":"from-woken-turn"}
19:31:06.995  toolResult sessions_spawn  accepted  childSessionKey=agent:main:subagent:61a17295-…
19:31:07.206  toolResult admin__reset   isError "Tool admin__reset not found"
admin server: no tools/call
control, same config, CLI sender (not alice), session agent:main:s2ctl:
19:38:41.052  provider  producer  tools=71  admin__reset=yes
19:38:48.506  admin     tools/call reset {"reason":"from-woken-turn"}
```

The denial applied only to alice's run, and the senderless woken turn inherited it: `admin__reset` was absent from the woken turn's tools and its call was refused. The same config still gave `admin__reset` to a non-alice sender, so the denial is sender-scoped and not global.

**S3: inherited restrictions in a spawned child** (children spawned from the S1 and S2 woken turns)

```text
S1 child agent:main:subagent:0e4cffe3-…
18:56:00.479  provider  child  offered=exec,fixture__echo,process,read,sessions_spawn,skills_read   -> fixture__echo
18:56:00.488  fixture   tools/call echo {"text":"from-child"}
18:56:00.505  toolResult admin__reset   isError "Tool admin__reset not found"
S2 child agent:main:subagent:61a17295-…
19:31:10.113  provider  child  tools=51  fixture__echo=yes  admin__reset=no   -> fixture__echo
19:31:10.254  fixture   tools/call echo {"text":"from-child"}
19:31:10.536  toolResult admin__reset   isError "Tool admin__reset not found"
admin server: no tools/call in either run
```

A child spawned from a woken turn keeps that turn's MCP access (`fixture__echo` works) and its restrictions: the S1 global cap and alice's denial still exclude `admin__reset`.

**S4: revocation after capture, before the woken turn** (S1 config; session `agent:main:s4`; exec `sleep 240`)

```text
19:10:29.444  provider  producer  offered=exec,fixture__echo,process,read,sessions_spawn,skills_read   -> exec {"command":"sleep 240; …","background":true}
19:10:30Z     producer turn returned (agent exit 0; exec still running, its completion target captured while fixture__echo was allowed)
19:11:52.750  gateway   config.patch write changedPaths=tools.deny            (tools.deny: ["fixture__echo"])
19:11:52.877  gateway   [reload] config hot reload applied (tools.deny)
19:29:59.180  transcript user "Exec completed (oceanic-, code 0) :: PROOF_EXEC_DONE"
19:30:02.327  provider  woken     offered=exec,process,read,sessions_spawn,skills_read   -> fixture__echo
19:30:02.575  toolResult fixture__echo  isError "Tool fixture__echo not found"
fixture server: last tools/call at 18:56:00.818 (S1), none after the revocation
```

The cap captured `fixture__echo`, but the woken turn applied its own current policy. After the hot-reloaded `tools.deny` the tool was not offered, and the call was rejected before any `tools/call` reached the fixture server.

Discovery (`initialize`/`tools/list`) still connects both configured servers during each run, as on `main`; policy filters tools, not discovery.

prs.title: fix(talk): apply Talk thinking level and Fast mode to STT/TTS replies
prs.body:
Related: #204661

Part 2 of 3 for #204661 (Talk settings page redesign). Sibling: #204674.

## What Problem This Solves

Talk thinking and Fast mode apply to Live consults, but speech-to-text plus voice currently uses the conversation preferences instead. Switching modes can therefore change how the same Talk agent replies.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Split Talk marks its `chat.send` with `useTalkSettings: true`. The Gateway, which already owns the Talk config, applies `consultThinkingLevel` / `consultFastMode` to that turn only when the request doesn't set `thinking` / `fastMode` itself. Explicit per-request values still win; plain chat and dictation are untouched.
- The Gateway applies the values (not the client), so every client gets identical behavior and no client needs to read Talk config to send a turn. It reuses the existing thinking-level normalization path (`normalizeThinkingLevelOverride`).
- Version skew: the Gateway advertises a `talk-chat-settings` server capability. Native clients (iOS, macOS, Android) send the flag only when it is advertised, since they update independently of the Gateway. The Control UI ships with its Gateway and sends the flag directly, with no older-Gateway fallback (`ui/AGENTS.md`, Gateway Coupling).
- Protocol schema, generated predicates and `docs/nodes/talk.md` updated for the new field.

## User Impact

- Thinking level and Fast mode set for Talk now apply to STT/TTS Talk replies too, matching Live.
- Unset settings change nothing. Per-request overrides keep priority.
- Native Talk clients (iOS, macOS, Android) also send the flag when the connected Gateway advertises `talk-chat-settings`, so their STT/TTS replies follow the Talk settings too. Against an older Gateway they send nothing and behave as before.

### Owner decision

> Should existing Talk consult thinking and Fast mode preferences override session preferences for browser and native STT/TTS turns?

**Owner decision: yes.** Configured Talk thinking and Fast mode override the session's for Talk turns in both modes, exactly as Live consults already do. Owner (Peter, 24 Nov): "no reason to have it for live but not STT/TTS". Design for the Talk settings revamp in #204661. Thinking and Fast mode belong to the Talk agent across Live consults and speech-to-text plus voice; the mode switch should not change which Talk preferences apply. An explicit turn override still wins. If Talk preferences are unset, keep session/model inheritance. Only Talk-originated turns opt in; ordinary chat and its saved preferences are unchanged. The decision is the PR author's and project owner's, not a claim of upstream maintainer approval.

### Upgrade from latest stable v2026.11.10 (same state; product code a76bcc15ee7)

> Review: *latest-stable upgrade proof* / *Add data-model compatibility proof*.

v2026.11.10 wrote the Talk config and created a session, with thinking high and fast on. The PR build then started on the same state directory. It sent two real turns on that session, one with `useTalkSettings:true` and one without.

Both starts report the same stored-config hash prefix. The config projections compared equal byte-for-byte; the stable and upgraded session rows also compared equal before either candidate turn. `<same-session>` replaces the same UUID throughout.

```text
commit=? config=4b28c5f2b446 
stop
commit=a76bcc15ee7 config=4b28c5f2b446 
stable config get talk: {"consultThinkingLevel":"low","consultFastMode":false,"realtime":{"mode":"stt-tts","provider":"xai"}}
candidate config get talk: {"consultThinkingLevel":"low","consultFastMode":false,"realtime":{"mode":"stt-tts","provider":"xai"}}
{"phase":"stable","version":"2026.11.10","talkChatSettings":false}
{"phase":"stable","rpc":"sessions.create","params":{"key":"agent:main:talk683-upgrade-check","model":"opencode-go/gpt-5.6-luna","thinkingLevel":"high","fastMode":true},"ok":true}
{"phase":"stable","rpc":"sessions.list","key":"agent:main:talk683-upgrade-check","sessionId":"<same-session>","thinkingLevel":"high","fastMode":true,"modelProvider":"opencode-go","model":"gpt-5.6-luna"}
{"phase":"upgraded","version":"2026.11.9","talkChatSettings":true}
{"phase":"upgraded","rpc":"sessions.list","key":"agent:main:talk683-upgrade-check","sessionId":"<same-session>","thinkingLevel":"high","fastMode":true,"modelProvider":"opencode-go","model":"gpt-5.6-luna"}
{"phase":"turns","version":"2026.11.9","talkChatSettings":true}
{"phase":"turns","rpc":"sessions.list","key":"agent:main:talk683-upgrade-check","sessionId":"<same-session>","thinkingLevel":"high","fastMode":true,"modelProvider":"opencode-go","model":"gpt-5.6-luna"}
{"phase":"turns","rpc":"chat.send","params":{"sessionKey":"agent:main:talk683-upgrade-check","message":"Reply with only OK. Do not use tools.","idempotencyKey":"talk683-v110-talk","useTalkSettings":true},"runId":"talk683-v110-talk","status":"started"}
{"phase":"turns","event":"chat","runId":"talk683-v110-talk","state":"final"}
{"phase":"turns","rpc":"chat.send","params":{"sessionKey":"agent:main:talk683-upgrade-check","message":"Reply with only OK. Do not use tools.","idempotencyKey":"talk683-v110-plain"},"runId":"talk683-v110-plain","status":"started"}
{"phase":"turns","event":"chat","runId":"talk683-v110-plain","state":"final"}
{"phase":"turns","rpc":"sessions.list","key":"agent:main:talk683-upgrade-check","sessionId":"<same-session>","thinkingLevel":"high","fastMode":true,"modelProvider":"opencode-go","model":"gpt-5.6-luna"}
{"type": "trace.metadata", "runId": "talk683-v110-talk", "thinkLevel": "low", "fastMode": false}
{"type": "trace.metadata", "runId": "talk683-v110-plain", "thinkLevel": "high", "fastMode": true}
```

The trajectory export truncated two long JSONL records, so they were not parsed as complete JSON. The reported fields are the allowlisted `runId`, `thinkLevel` and `fastMode` extracted from the two `trace.metadata` records and matched exactly to the run IDs acknowledged by the Gateway. No raw trajectory, auth material, prompt context, response body, or endpoint is included.

- The candidate opened the same state as published v2026.11.10 without regenerating config, preserved the Talk config and saved session, and newly advertised `talk-chat-settings`.
- Both real Gateway turns reached `final`. The opted-in run used Talk's **low / false**; an otherwise identical unflagged run used the session's **high / true**. Session settings still read **high / true** afterwards.
- This exercises the Gateway from RPC admission through run preference resolution. It does not exercise a native caller, mic/STT, TTS playback, the Talk realtime provider, inference latency differences, or other models/configurations. The candidate is identified by commit, not by the numerically lower embedded version string.

Head `fd82630f1bc` is an empty commit on `a76bcc15ee7`. It re-runs CI, because the previous macOS dead-code jobs failed on hosted SwiftPM dependency checkouts rather than on this code.

## Evidence

Shipped Control UI, headless Chromium, synthetic microphone WAV and local CLI transcription fixture. Captured outgoing request and acknowledged response:

```text
{"request": "talk.session.create", "params": {"mode": "transcription", "transport": "gateway-relay"}}
{"response": "talk.session.create", "ok": true, "sessionCreated": true}
{"request": "chat.send", "params": {"useTalkSettings": true}}
{"response": "chat.send", "ok": true}
{"event": "trace.metadata", "thinkLevel": "low", "fastMode": false}
```




- The browser split-Talk harness drives the production caller from a synthetic final transcript to `chat.send` and checks that the caller sets `useTalkSettings: true`. All 21 focused browser tests passed. Removing the marker in the production caller failed both transcript cases. The Gateway transport and audio are test fixtures; this does not establish a live native caller run.
- Same-state restart from the published v2026.11.9 Gateway to the patched build: both loaded STT/TTS, thinking `low`, and Fast mode `false` from byte-identical config. Only the patched Gateway advertised `talk-chat-settings`.

  | Gateway | Talk mode | Thinking | Fast mode | Advertises `talk-chat-settings` |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | v2026.11.9 | STT/TTS | low | false | no |
  | Patched | STT/TTS | low | false | yes |

- Gateway negative control: with only the request normalizer replaced by its unmodified base version, both opted-in preference cases failed (thinking was unset instead of `low` and `off`). Restoring the patched normalizer passed both cases.


### Native iPhone turns against a real Gateway (26 Nov 2026)

> Review: *native execution remains fixture-backed; add one native production-path capture*.

- **Phone:** a physical iPhone running a device build of this PR's code (OC 102513: main `b48d578d023` plus this PR at `fd82630f1bc`).
- **Gateway:** a real Gateway build that carries this PR.
- **Chat preferences:** thinking **high**, Fast mode **off**.
- **Talk config:** `talk.consultThinkingLevel: "low"`, `talk.consultFastMode: true`, `talk.realtime.mode: "stt-tts"`.

The tester spoke four Talk turns in STT/TTS mode, then sent one typed message in the same chat. The table shows the runtime preferences that the Gateway stored on each run (`__openclaw.chatSendRuntime`), taken from a redacted `openclaw sessions export-trajectory`:

| Time (UTC) | Path | Reply | `chatSendRuntime.thinking` | `chatSendRuntime.fastMode` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 04:25:22 | iPhone Talk (spoken) | 12. | `low` | `true` |
| 04:25:59 | iPhone Talk (spoken) | 81. | `low` | `true` |
| 04:29:11 | iPhone Talk (spoken) | 100. | `low` | `true` |
| 04:29:29 | iPhone Talk (spoken) | 121. | `low` | `true` |
| 04:51:48 | iPhone typed message | 169. | `high` | (absent, so the chat's Fast off applies) |

The native STT/TTS caller sent the Talk-settings request, so those runs used Talk's low/true. The typed message in the same chat kept the conversation's own high/off. The chat's saved preferences were not changed: `sessions.list` still reports high/false.

Limits: iPhone only (macOS and Android were not exercised). The tester observed the spoken path on the device and did not record it on screen for this check. Values come from the Gateway's stored run metadata, not from the provider's request body.

### iOS simulator caller proof

The production iOS `TalkModeManager` push-to-talk path received a fixture transcript and submitted `chat.send` through its real Gateway client. A test-only patch observed the outgoing WebSocket request; the Gateway handshake and replies were fixtures. Both cases of `TalkModeManagerTests.native Talk sends settings marker only when Gateway advertises support` passed:

```text
capability present (true):  useTalkSettings == true   PASS
capability absent  (false): useTalkSettings omitted   PASS
SIM_TESTS=xctest=0 swift-testing=52 rc=0
STATUS=PASS
```

Simulator job: `talk-native-204683-r1` (`run.log`, `out/sim-tests.xcresult`). This verifies iOS caller gating, not a live older Gateway or a native model turn. The separate Gateway trace below covers preference resolution. macOS and Android callers were not exercised.

Native send-path proof (production `TalkModeManager` push-to-talk through its real Gateway client; fixture transcript and fixture Gateway handshake, outgoing `chat.send` frame captured; job `talk-settings-native-r3`, `TalkChatSettingsSendTests`, 2 cases, `SIM_TESTS=xctest=0 swift-testing=1 rc=0`, head `ea196847ac3`). Redacted frames (idempotency keys omitted):

```text
Gateway advertises talk-chat-settings:
  chat.send {"message":"Talk Mode active. Reply in a concise, spoken tone.\n\nWhat is the time?","sessionKey":"agent:main:talk-settings-test","useTalkSettings":true}
Gateway does not advertise it:
  chat.send {"message":"Talk Mode active. Reply in a concise, spoken tone.\n\nWhat is the time?","sessionKey":"agent:main:talk-settings-test"}
```

No `thinking` or `fastMode` is sent by the client in either case; the Gateway resolves them (see the runtime trace below). This is a simulator run against a fixture Gateway, not a live native model turn. macOS and Android callers were not exercised.

Focused Gateway tests:
- `src/gateway/server-methods/chat-send-request.test.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.directive-tags.test.ts`: 2 files, 196 tests passed. Covers applied vs not applied by the flag, unset values, and explicit Fast mode true/false. Includes "keeps explicit per-request thinking and Fast mode over Talk settings" (request `thinking: high, fastMode: true` beats Talk `low` / `false`).
- oxfmt and oxlint clean on touched files.

Runtime proof (isolated proof Gateway on this branch, real model turns on `claude-cli/claude-sonnet-5-5`; config `talk.consultThinkingLevel: low`, `talk.consultFastMode: false`; the session `agent:main:proof-split` is set to thinking `high` + Fast mode on). The turns were sent over the Gateway WebSocket as `chat.send`; the values below come from each run's `trace.metadata` event in the runtime trajectory:

| run | `chat.send` | resolved thinking | resolved Fast mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| `proof-plain-5` | plain chat | `high` | `true` |
| `proof-talk-1` | `useTalkSettings: true` (split STT/TTS turn) | `low` | `false` |
| `proof-plain-6` | plain chat, same session, after the Talk turn | `high` | `true` |

After all three turns `sessions.list` still reports the session as thinking `high`, Fast mode `true`: the Talk values apply to that one turn only, and plain chat is unchanged.

prs.title: feat(ios): sent videos play inline in the chat
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On iPhone, a video sent in a chat shows as a black card with a large play button. It has no picture until it plays, and it doesn't say how long it is. The Control UI shows a sent video's first frame in place and plays it right there in the conversation.

## User Impact

This is one of a series of pull requests that bring the iOS app's chat in line with the Control UI. With this change alone, a person on iPhone sees:

- A sent video shows its first frame above the message bubble, at the video's own shape and in the same width limit as sent photos, with its length in the corner (for example "0:06").
- Tapping the frame plays the video in place with the system player controls. Only one video plays at a time. A video stops when it scrolls out of view or when the app goes to the background.
- While a video is still sending, its frame comes from the phone's own copy, so it shows right away. After that, the frame and the playback come from the Gateway's stored copy of the video.
- When Talk mode holds media playback, the video shows "Pause Talk mode before playing this attachment." instead of playing.
- A video the app can't load, or one the Gateway didn't store as a managed video, keeps the existing file card.
- VoiceOver reads the frame as "Play video" with the video's length as its value.

Some parts still look old until later pull requests in the series:
- A video that is still sending isn't dimmed and shows no upload state.
- The composer's attach sheet isn't updated yet.

The inline player is iOS only. macOS keeps the existing video card, which this change only refactors (a new initializer that takes a URL), and the macOS app wasn't checked.

## Why This Change Was Made

A sent video should look like what was sent, the way photos already do, and play without leaving the conversation. The app now reads a video's display size, duration and first frame when you attach it, and keeps the sent copy for that send, so the box takes its final size before anything loads and the transcript doesn't move. The transcript plays one video at a time through a shared owner (`ChatInlineVideos`), so starting another video, scrolling away or backgrounding the app stops the current one. Playback asks the Gateway for a fresh stream when you tap and reuses bytes it already downloaded.

## Evidence

- Unit tests on an iPhone simulator (iOS 27.2): `ChatMediaImageBoxTests` and `SwiftUIRenderSmokeTests`, 24 passed, 0 failed. They cover when a video is shown inline (it needs dimensions and either the local copy or a managed artifact) and that managed previews use their playback route while audio waits for a tap.
- The iOS app and its test bundles build with the SwiftFormat and strict SwiftLint build phases. `scripts/lint-swift.sh ios` and `scripts/format-swift.sh ios` report no violations. The native i18n sync reports `changed=false`.
- Screenshots: a chat with one synthetic sent video (a 6-second gradient clip served by the demo transport), a caption and an assistant reply. They were taken in screenshot mode on the same simulator, before and after, in light (paused, and playing after a tap on the video) and dark (paused). Before is the series up to the previous pull request, not `main`. The demo history, the clip and the screenshot test were added only for these runs and aren't part of this change.
- Not checked:
  - Videos sent to or loaded from a real Gateway, including the stream ticket on tap and the download fallback.
  - The Talk mode message, which needs Talk mode running.
  - Stopping on scroll and on backgrounding, by hand.
  - VoiceOver on a device.
  - The macOS app.
  - A physical device.

Before is on the left and After on the right in each image.

![Light: a sent video with a caption. Before, it is a black card with a play button. After, it shows its first frame above the bubble with "0:06" in the corner.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/12273868-8998-4cdc-8416-0b0142513c82)

![Light: the same video playing in place after a tap, before and after.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ea338515-a6cf-4d3f-bf3b-b9df53a634ba)

![Dark: the same chat. Before, the black card with a play button. After, the first frame with "0:06" in the corner.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9ed2f8f2-0499-44ce-9723-f743966f23b9)

prs.title: improve: reduce memory needed to renew the Gateway lock
prs.body:
Related to https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/192547.

## What Problem This Solves

Every Gateway starts a worker to renew its lock file. The worker loaded database query and recovery code before its first renewal, even though renewing a held file only needs its lock payload and filesystem identity.

## User Impact

The Gateway can renew its file lock sooner and with less memory. The same worker still rejects a replacement file. Doctor and update recovery keep their synchronous database check before deciding that a legacy Gateway has stopped.

## Why This Change Was Made

Lock acquisition and recovery own the inspection of the legacy SQLite lease. Moving that classifier to its callers keeps its query, stale-owner rules and error handling intact. The heartbeat can use the existing parser independently.

## Evidence

Both production worker configurations were built on the same source base. On macOS arm64 with Node 26.13.1, each worker renewed a real temporary lock file in a fresh process. Ten alternating stock/candidate pairs per build produced the following medians. The memory columns give the median within-pair reduction at the first renewal.

| Worker build | First renewal, stock → candidate | Process RSS reduction | Worker V8 physical heap reduction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary | 126.6 → 21.3 ms | 50.3 MiB | 36.1 MiB |
| Sealed | 45.6 → 15.2 ms | 16.4 MiB | 5.4 MiB |

All ten pairs improved in each column for both builds. The ordinary worker went from 884,354 to 120,643 emitted bytes and the sealed worker from 1,183,398 to 120,322. Across all 48 runs the worker renewed the original inode, rejected a same-content replacement and exited cleanly. Maintenance fixtures also distinguished a live launcher from a lost parent.

The shared-state reader finishes its assertions and then loses a worker cleanup acknowledgement ([base report](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/207065), [PR job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46092085306/job/140815640664)). Follow-up to #206900.

## What Problem This Solves

A restart sent 719 bytes of instructions, or 937 if a shell result was missing. The longer prompt suggested an extra lookup. “Continue independent work” could sound like an instruction to leave the original request unfinished.

- Restart instruction without a run ID: **719 → 374 bytes** normally; **937 → 420 bytes** with a missing shell result. Before #206900, the missing-result case paused the turn without calling the model.

prs.title: fix(imap): require the authenticated From mailbox to match the allowlisted sender
prs.body:
## Problem

The IMAP email trigger decides admission in two steps: the allowlist matches the sender address that `mailparser` reads from the From header, and `mailauth` evaluates DMARC/DKIM/SPF from its own parse of the same raw bytes. The two parsers follow different rules for header syntax, so a crafted From header can make them read different mailboxes: the allowlist matches an allowlisted address while the authentication result describes a different, attacker-controlled mailbox that a DKIM signature at the attacker's own domain aligns with. Such a message can pass the authentication floor and reach agent dispatch logged as `strength=verified` with the allowlisted domain.

## Solution

An accepted verdict that relies on a `mailauth` result additionally requires that `mailauth` read exactly one From mailbox (`result.dkim.headerFrom`) and that it equals the mailbox which matched `allowedSenders`. A mismatch, an absent From mailbox, or more than one rejects permanently with `gate=sender-mismatch`, so the message is skipped and logged like other gate rejections.

The local part is compared exactly after removing optional quotes around a plain dot-atom local part, so correctly signed mail whose From is `"trusted"@example.com` still matches `trusted@example.com`; a quoted string that carries anything a local part cannot carry unquoted stays as written. Domains are compared case-insensitively in their punycode (A-label) form, so an allowlist entry configured with a Unicode IDN domain still matches a header that spells it as punycode. The sender-bound token path and the DNS-failure fallback, which have no `mailauth` result to compare, are unchanged.

## Impact

Only deployments with the opt-in IMAP trigger enabled and an `allowedSenders` account are affected. Mail with a From header the two parsers read differently is admitted only when the authenticated mailbox is exactly the allowlisted sender; anything ambiguous is rejected instead of dispatched.

## Tests

- New watcher test drives the loopback IMAP server with real `mailauth` verification and fixture DNS over four messages: an allowlisted sender dispatches as verified, a message whose From header the two parsers read differently is rejected with `gate=sender-mismatch`, an unknown sender is rejected as before, and a legit reply still dispatches.
- New watcher test covers an allowlisted IDN sender whose header spells the domain in punycode and dispatches as verified. New watcher tests cover a sender whose From local part is quoted, ASCII or SMTPUTF8, and dispatches as verified.
- `extensions/imap` vitest suite: 83 passed. Typecheck (`tsgo` extensions lane), oxlint, and format pass on the touched files.
- End-to-end proof on a real Gateway on a Crabbox AWS runner: a Dovecot IMAP server, local DNS with fixture DMARC/DKIM records, and a local model endpoint. On the base commit the crafted message dispatches to the reader agent; on this head, restarting the Gateway on the same account (upgrade path) rejects the crafted message with `gate=sender-mismatch`, dispatches ordinary, IDN, and quoted-local-part signed mail with completed agent runs, and replays nothing from before the restart. Details in the evidence comment.

prs.title: feat(ios): the chat header shows the agent and title, a more menu, and fits landscape
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On iPhone, the chat header shows a small avatar with a status dot and a centered chat name, and its `…` button opens a large popover that mixes model settings, display options, Export chat, Gateway settings and New session options. The Control UI shows who you are talking to and what the chat is called at the top of the chat, and keeps chat actions such as pin, rename, move and delete in one short menu. In landscape, the iPhone header and transcript leave little room for long chat titles and the first message.

## User Impact

This is one of a series of pull requests that bring the iOS app's chat in line with the Control UI. With this change alone, a person on iPhone sees:

- In the main chat, the header shows the agent's avatar and name in the middle, and the transcript scrolls beneath it.
- In any other chat, the header shows the avatar next to the chat's title, with the project name under it when the chat belongs to one. Long titles stay on one line in landscape, between the sidebar button and the `…` button.
- The `…` button opens a short **Chat actions** menu: **New Chat**, **Pin** or **Unpin**, **Rename…**, **Move to group** (with **New group…** and **Remove from group**), **Context usage**, **Archive** and **Delete…**. Rename and new group use a text alert; Delete asks for confirmation first. If a change fails, an alert says so.
- Model, thinking, Fast mode and tool detail settings no longer appear in that menu. New session options open from the composer (type `/new`), and Gateway settings open from the sidebar.
- The composer placeholder reads "Message Molty" (with the agent's name), and the empty chat no longer shows starter prompts.
- In landscape, the header fits the compact toolbar and the transcript scrolls beneath the composer.
- The iOS docs no longer say that Chat actions show or hide reasoning and tool activity; they point to **Settings → Chat** for that choice.

Some parts of these screens still look old until later pull requests in the series: the sidebar button has no round glass background yet, your own messages still show their date underneath, tapping the agent name does not open a chat info page yet, and subagent chats do not have their own header yet. Because there is no chat info page yet, Rename and Archive stay in the menu for now. The **Settings → Chat** page the docs mention, with the reasoning and tool activity choice, arrives with a later pull request; until then that choice is not in the app.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Control UI already separates who and what you are chatting with (the header) from what you can do with the chat (a short actions menu), and keeps model and session settings next to the composer. Matching that on iPhone makes the header readable at a glance and the menu short enough to scan. The menu's sections come from one tested function, `ChatActionsMenu.sections`, so which rows a chat gets (saved or new, main or not, archivable, deletable, with context usage or not) is decided in one place. The landscape changes use the compact system toolbar and a shared keyboard padding so the header and composer leave room for the transcript.

## Evidence

- Unit tests on an iPhone 17 Pro simulator (iOS 27.2): `ChatActionsMenuTests`, plus `ChatTypingFocusTests`, `SidebarDrawerGesturePolicyTests` and `GatewayStatusBuilderTests`, which build the chat screen. 31 passed, 0 failed.
- UI tests on the same simulator: `testChatActionsAndNewSessionOptionsHaveSeparateEntryPoints`, `testChatToolbarFitsCurrentWindow`, `testNewSessionOptionsRemainReachableAtAccessibilitySize`, `testLandscapeLongProjectChatTitleFitsBetweenControls`, `testLandscapeNormalHeaderShowsNameBesideAvatar` and `testLandscapeTranscriptScrollsBeneathComposer` passed.
- UI test `testPhoneOfflineChatKeepsCompactLayout` fails at its last step, twice in a row: with the sidebar open over Settings, a tap on the visible part of Settings reaches the Settings list (it opens Storage) instead of closing the sidebar. The same test passes on the finished series. Closing the sidebar on such a tap belongs to the sidebar drawer, which a later pull request in the series replaces; this change does not touch the drawer.
- The iOS app and its UI test bundle build with the SwiftFormat and strict SwiftLint build phases. `scripts/lint-swift.sh ios` and `scripts/format-swift.sh ios` report no violations. `native:i18n:verify` reports `changed=false`. `git diff --check` is clean.
- Screenshots: the same demo chats in screenshot mode on the same simulator, before and after, in light (main chat, titled chat, Chat actions menu, landscape) and dark (main chat). Before is the series up to the previous pull request, not `main`. No Gateway or account data.
- Not checked: subagent chat headers (they need a later pull request), the menu's actions against a live Gateway, iPad, VoiceOver on a device, and a physical device.

Before is on the left and After on the right in each image.

prs.title: fix: preserve source ranges in compaction requests
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A plugin that screens tool results and outside-user messages can distinguish them during a normal embedded turn. When those entries are included in a generated compaction request, the plugin receives one synthetic user message and loses those source boundaries.

## User Impact

Compaction plugins can use the existing `contextSpans` field to screen rendered tool results and recorded outside-user input while preserving adjacent owner text and summary instructions. The prompt bytes and compaction budgets stay the same when the plugin leaves the payload as it is.

## Why This Change Was Made

Record each range when the bounded serializer knows which source entry it rendered. That works for sampled and elided entries and for batched transcript reads. The existing final-request hook exposes the ranges through the same carrier mechanism it uses for in-history system updates.

## Evidence

The provider regression fails on the base and passes with the patch. The same text appears in an owner message, a tool result, an outside-user message, and the summary instructions. The regression replaces only the two tagged copies in the actual encoded OpenAI Responses request.

## Summary

### High Level TLDR

Keep track of where tool results and outside-user messages land in a generated summary request so plugins can screen the right text.

## Root Cause

`serializeConversationWithinBudget` and the worker renderer join tool results and user messages into one text body. `createSummarizationContext` wraps that body in one synthetic user message. The request hook saw the right request kind but received no source offsets. On the base, the provider regression failed before sending because its hook could find no labelled copies.

## Verification

- `pnpm test test/model-request-provider-policy.test.ts` passed all 14 tests on the patch. Running the new test alone on the base failed at the request-body assertion.
- `pnpm test packages/agent-core/src/harness/compaction/utils.test.ts packages/agent-core/src/harness/compaction/summarization-input-budget.test.ts` passed all 51 tests. Existing serialization hashes still match, and the same test now checks offsets on full, sampled, and trimmed inputs.
- Prepared compaction passed all 21 tests. The hook and provider text-transform suites passed all 9 tests. `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:test:root`, focused formatting and lint, and `git diff --check` passed. The isolated build passed. The final inventory change removes a retired source path. Wrapper closure passed 24 tests and PR source provisioning passed 17, with two platform skips.
- Local renderer benchmark on Node 26.13.1, 30 warmups and 100 interleaved samples per case. For 60 turns, p50/p95 changed from 0.267/0.458 ms to 0.270/0.453 ms. For 800 turns, p50/p95 changed from 3.491/4.917 ms to 3.363/5.026 ms. Both cases produced byte-identical summary text.

## Real behavior proof

Run `pnpm test test/model-request-provider-policy.test.ts -t 'keeps rendered source ranges'`. It uses the core summarization path, real hook runner and Responses request encoder, intercepting network I/O at the provider boundary. Base output showed `Number of calls: 0` because the test hook required source ranges. With the patch, one encoded request arrived containing the owner copy, two replacement markers, and the original summary instructions.

An isolated Gateway ran the built runtime with a disposable transcript, a deterministic policy hook, and a real local OpenAI-compatible model. `openclaw sessions compact agent:main:main --timeout 90000 --json` returned `"compacted": true`. The hook logged that it rewrote two source ranges. A transcript readback confirmed that the persisted summary still held the owner request and omitted both tagged copies.

## What was not tested

The isolated Gateway uses a fixture policy hook. This change covers the host-generated history prompt. Provider-native checkpoints, summaries persisted by earlier versions, and extension-owned summary prompts were outside this proof.

prs.title: fix: converge plugins after every Gateway boot
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin maintenance currently depends on an updater trial. Replacing OpenClaw through an image swap, global package install, manual Git pull, or standalone binary can leave installed plugins behind the serving core.

## User Impact

Every Gateway boot starts plugin convergence in the background after core readiness. Active trials defer the work. Changed plugins reload through the existing lifecycle; plugin failures do not delay readiness or change the core update outcome.

Boot maintenance is unattended and no longer inherits `openclaw update --accept-capabilities` consent from the trial. A plugin that widens capabilities is declined; the existing failed plugin step retains its capability-review guidance and exact `openclaw plugins update <id>` recovery command. Ordinary offline boots create no update run or failure notice.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Delete `maintainTrialPlugins` and the trial-keyed plugin scheduler; reuse the existing watcher, ten-minute child command, lifecycle lease, and batch reload.
- Use existing update history only to attribute completed plugin output to the serving build, never to decide whether convergence runs.
- Keep advisory Doctor inspections updater-only. The Docker entrypoint Doctor/capture deletion is deliberately outside this PR.
- No new persisted state, markers, statuses, notices, locks, flags, or retries.
- Runtime-only scope: **−4 production lines**, +63 unit-test lines, documentation updated. No survivor scenario, catalog, registry, or harness changes.

## Evidence

- Red on `ea77ca3d602c` in an isolated `ocx base --src`: ordinary/no-trial and offline boot cases fail because the plugin child is never called; pending/trial/restoring cases pass.
- The regression exercises the existing Gateway core-ready boundary, not a direct scheduler call.
- Merged-head stable-to-head gate: [Package Acceptance 46091303769](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46091303769), candidate `abbbf6eefa5701c63669eafaf89c23b28f0116f3`, baseline `openclaw@2026.11.10`, existing `update-restart-auth` lane.
- Baseline comparison: [current-main b7e36af75284 passed the same lane](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46086533588); [the old-base 42037bdcea59 candidate failed in old-updater Doctor admission](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46079640633). Current main `94ae31d8491d` is now merged before rerunning; the old-base failure is not classified as inherited or isolated to this change.
- The narrowed history guard preserves an already settled plugin step across later offline boots. All 3 focused owner regression cases passed; scoped core lint had 0 warnings and 0 errors.
- Earlier Docker seed CI reached its unchanged 55-minute outer limit after healthy, crash/rollback, and enforced downgrade receipts reported passing. No failing runtime assertion was recorded.
- The separate Doctor-free manual-swap proof PR #206999 is not a prerequisite for this runtime PR or PR 4.
- Review findings are repaired or explicitly rejected: ordinary failures use the existing warning log, notice errors cannot skip convergence, live details refresh, and settled history is not rewritten. Trial consent remains intentionally absent from this boot job.
- Current-head hosted validation is pending. No local full build was run; the stalled Boat wrapper was cancelled before allocation.

prs.title: fix(update): clean up rejected Git update worktrees
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A dev-channel Git update can build successfully and then fail its candidate release checks. The updater deletes the staging files but leaves Git pointing at the deleted worktree.

## User Impact

Rejected candidates are removed from both disk and Git's worktree inventory. The serving checkout and unrelated worktrees stay intact, and admitted candidates retain their registration at the published release path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing `prepareUpdate` staging owner now unregisters the selected Git worktree before deleting unpublished staging. Git and package builders return their diagnostics without competing staging cleanup paths.

Production: +11/-10, net +1 line, to carry the selected checkout through post-build rejection. Tests: +73/-12, net +61 lines. Published-release registration repair and trial custody retain their current owner.

## Evidence

- RED: the real-Git regression fails with the previous production code after a completed build and refused release check; Git reports a registration whose directory no longer exists.
- GREEN: 54/54 tests across `src/update/prepare-failure.test.ts` and `src/update/prepare.test.ts`. Coverage includes build failure, late candidate rejection, unrelated worktrees, published registration, package preparation, and native-binding failures.

The remote source patch was verified by SHA-256 before and after execution; its seven changed files match `08ef8467fee4e7e4c8f196e87110ccc93b32d765`. prs.title: fix(docker): skip no-op chmod calls in the build stage permission steps (#199340)
prs.body:
Fixes #199340.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Docker source rebuilds spend tens of seconds in two permission steps that change nothing, whenever `COPY . .` misses the cache on an overlayfs builder.

## User Impact

User impact: source rebuilds of the Docker image finish those two steps in well under a second, and the resulting image has the same file modes and ownership as before. No action is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

After `COPY . .`, the Dockerfile's `build` stage runs two permission steps that call `chmod` on every entry under `/app` (except `node_modules`) and on every plugin and agent file. Most entries already have the target mode. On overlayfs, even a no-op `chmod` copies the file up into the new layer, so every `COPY . .` cache miss pays for about 64k copy-ups and the layer comes out the same.

Both steps now call `chmod` only on entries whose mode would change:

- **Source step (`a+rX`):** skips directories that already have `-perm -0555` and regular files that already have `-perm -0444` and either all or no execute bits (`X` adds execute for all only when some execute bit is set). Every other entry still reaches `chmod a+rX`.
- **Plugin and agent step:** `! -perm 0755` for directories and `! -perm 0644` for files. These are exact matches, so special bits still get cleared as before.
- **Symlinks:** the skip conditions match only `-type d` and `-type f`, so symlinks still reach `chmod`. It follows them to their targets as before, and a dangling symlink still fails the step.
- **Portability:** the predicates use POSIX `-perm` forms only (no GNU `-perm /0111`), so the regression test runs with both BSD and GNU `find`.

## Evidence

### Regression test

`src/dockerfile.test.ts` replaces the old string match with a test that runs the Dockerfile's own two `RUN` commands. It applies them to a fixture tree through a `chmod` shim that logs its arguments. The tree contains 0000, 0600, 0744, 0755, 4755 and 0644 files, 0700 directories, plugin files and a symlink, plus a `node_modules` file that must stay at 0600.

The test asserts three things:
- every entry ends at the expected mode;
- only the entries that needed a change, plus the symlink, reach `chmod`;
- a second pass calls `chmod` only on the symlink.

On `main` it fails: 21 paths reach `chmod`, including the root and already-correct files. With the fix it passes, and the final modes match `main`'s for every fixture entry.

Local: `dockerfile.test.ts` 8/8 and `docker-build-cache.test.ts` 1/1. oxlint, oxfmt, `git diff --check` and the test-lines ratchet are clean.

### Docker on overlayfs

Docker 29.3.1 with the overlayfs driver on 16 CPUs. A proof Dockerfile starts from the build stage's pinned `node:24.22.1-trixie` image. It does `COPY . .` of this commit's `git archive` (863 MB, 64,291 entries after the copy) and adds a few mixed-mode files and a symlink. It then runs `main`'s or this PR's two steps, extracted verbatim from each Dockerfile, as separate timed `RUN` layers. The timed stage ran with `--no-cache-filter`:

```
== main step1 43086 ms  step2 29199 ms  entries=64291
== fix  step1   261 ms  step2   223 ms  entries=64291
== main step1 137983 ms step2 26761 ms  entries=64291
== fix  step1   120 ms  step2   102 ms  entries=64291
```

A sorted `find /app -printf '%m %u:%g %y %p\n'` dump after both steps is byte-identical between `main` and the fix across all 64,291 entries. The mixed-mode probes landed at 444, 644 and 755 as expected, setuid stayed 4755, and private directories went to 755.

With GNU findutils 4.10.0, a tree containing a dangling symlink fails the source step with `chmod: cannot operate on dangling symlink` and exit 1, on both `main` and the fix.

Not run: a full `docker buildx build` of the runtime image. Only these two `RUN` steps changed, and the proof runs them verbatim on the same base image and the same `COPY . .` input.

prs.title: feat(ios): photos sit above the bubble and open in a viewer that grows from the thumbnail
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On iPhone, the photos you send in a chat don't look like photos. Each one is a file row with an icon and its name, stacked inside your message bubble, and tapping it doesn't open anything. The Control UI shows sent images as images above the message, and opens them full screen. Images also have no reserved space while they load, so the transcript jumps when one arrives, and a failed image gives no way to try again.

## User Impact

This is one of a series of pull requests that bring the iOS app's chat in line with the Control UI. With this change alone, a person on iPhone sees:

- Photos you send sit above your message bubble, aligned to the right. One photo shows at its own shape, and several show as square tiles. Past four, a line says how many more aren't shown ("1 more image not shown", "3 more images not shown"). Other files show as cards above the bubble.
- Your bubble and the images on either side share one width limit, which leaves room on the opposite side of the column. Images in assistant replies use the same limit.
- Tapping an image opens a full-screen viewer that grows out of the thumbnail. The viewer has Close and Share buttons, shows the position ("1 of 3") when the message has several images, and has a row of thumbnails to move between them. You can zoom, and you can drag the fitted image down to close it. A photo you sent sharpens to the original in the viewer.
- Each image box takes its final size before the image loads, with a faint shimmer, so the transcript doesn't move when the image arrives. An image that fails to load says "Couldn’t load image." and offers **Try again**.
- Pasted photos and camera shots get a generated file name, and the viewer hides names the app made up. It shows a sent photo's file name only when you chose it.
- VoiceOver reads a sent photo as "Photo" (or its alt text), hints that it opens full screen, and reads each filmstrip thumbnail as "Image 1 of 3". A file card reads as one element.
- The iOS docs describe where attachments sit and how sent photos load.

Some parts still look old until later pull requests in the series:
- A photo that is still sending isn't dimmed and shows no upload ring.
- The time stays under the message instead of on the photo for a photo-only message.
- Sent videos don't play inline yet.
- The chat header and the composer aren't updated yet.

The bubble layout and the full-screen viewer are iOS-only. The macOS app shares some of the image box code and wasn't checked.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Control UI already shows images as images above the message and opens them in a viewer. Doing the same on iPhone makes a sent photo look like what was sent, and gives every image in the chat one way to open, zoom and share. Reserving each image's size before it loads keeps the transcript still while you read. Sent photos load from the phone's own copy while sending and from the Gateway's thumbnail afterward, and the viewer asks for the original only when you open it. Layout, gallery and viewer rules live in tested types: `ChatColumnLayout`, `ChatImageViewerItem` and `ChatMediaImageBox`.

## Evidence

- Unit tests on an iPhone simulator (iOS 27.2): `ChatMediaImageBoxTests`, 9 passed, 0 failed.
- OpenClawKit SwiftPM tests on macOS: `ChatColumnLayoutTests` and `ChatMediaImagePreviewTests` ("Chat image preview"), 12 passed, 0 failed.
- The iOS app and its test bundles build with the SwiftFormat and strict SwiftLint build phases. `scripts/lint-swift.sh ios` and `scripts/format-swift.sh ios` report no violations. `native:i18n:verify` reports `changed=false`, and `git diff --check` is clean.
- Screenshots: a chat with synthetic photos (three sent together with a caption, one sent alone, one damaged) and an assistant reply. They were taken in screenshot mode on the same simulator, before and after, in light (sent photos, a photo that fails to load, and the viewer opened from the first of three photos) and dark (transcript). Before is the series up to the previous pull request, not `main`. The demo history and the screenshot test were added only for these runs and aren't part of this change.
- Not checked:
  - Photos loaded from a real Gateway, including the original in the viewer and the thumbnail after a relaunch.
  - Share from the viewer.
  - Zoom and drag-to-close by hand.
  - VoiceOver on a device.
  - The macOS app.
  - A physical device.

Before is on the left and After on the right in each image.

![Light: three photos sent with a caption and one sent alone. Before, each is a file row inside the bubble. After, they are square tiles and a single photo above the bubble.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/184386ca-021c-42fd-9747-2acb2338f10c)

![Light: a photo that fails to load. Before, it is a file row like the others. After, its box says "Couldn’t load image." with Try again.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/021fae7c-5760-4f42-b073-d168ee3da02f)

![Light: tapping the first of three photos. Before, nothing opens. After, the viewer shows the photo with Close, Share, "1 of 3" and a row of thumbnails.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/07e23004-d071-4cfd-a768-b077f0aef3db)

![Dark: the same chat, scrolled to the single photo and the failed one, before and after.](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a3208dfd-3bf1-4e91-93f8-8a74d9343942)

prs.title: improve: reduce memory needed to load the model catalog
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Loading the model picker evaluates session-transcript and authority code in its catalog worker. A legacy memory plugin drags in that code at registration, before anyone opens a memory provider.

Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/192547

## User Impact

The packaged catalog worker loads 125 fewer JavaScript files. In a one-provider Linux ARM64 fixture, peak service memory fell from 225.08 to 216.16 MiB. This isolates one cost of loading the catalog. The full Gateway first-turn memory issue remains open.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the legacy manager adapter alongside its backend registration and import that same implementation when opening the selected legacy provider. Native provider handles retain their existing session authority, cancellation, handoff and cleanup owner. All six moved or remaining functions retain their bodies. Manager acquisition still starts synchronously when the legacy provider is opened. Production changes total +224/-225 lines and the regression test adds 41 lines.

## Evidence

- Built the normal packages at both ends of this change. The catalog worker's relative static import closure fell from 1,331 files (9,708,072 bytes) to 1,206 (8,842,389 bytes). The legacy adapter remains present. The native-bound memory adapter, session audience, transcript lease and delivery generation drop out of the closure.
- The new regression fails on the parent at the eager session-audience import and passes on the candidate. Existing SQLite-backed grant, delegated-child revocation, release, caller authority and provider lifecycle tests pass in both revisions (69 on the parent, 70 including the regression on the candidate). The actual packaged legacy adapter preserves immediate manager lookup, bound receivers, synchronous exceptions, abort reason, cached default managers and transient cleanup under Node and the repository-pinned Bun.
- Linux ARM64, Node 24.22.1, four fresh processes per arm in counterbalanced order, identical installed paths and one configured synthetic provider. Cold median 2,129 to 2,011 ms, settled Node PSS 194.87 to 186.37 MiB. In the first pair series, the median of a single warm call rose from 13.50 to 26.06 ms. A separate uninterrupted 24-call warm series found p50 8.91 to 8.62 ms and p95 39.71 to 33.42 ms. All 200 cold/warm catalog and runtime responses matched and all processes closed naturally.
- Darwin ARM64, Node 26.7.0, same physical install path, four fresh processes per arm. Median peak process RSS 320.12 to 312.88 MiB, settled RSS 283.59 to 274.41 MiB and catalog worker physical heap 64.13 to 60.68 MiB. Cold median 634 to 623 ms, later warm p50 2.45 to 2.52 ms and p95 3.42 to 3.97 ms. All 200 results matched. Reversing the arm order and running 150 warm calls per process produced 1,208 matching cold/warm results. The median per-process total for 150 calls was 375.72 to 376.29 ms. Pooled warm p50 was 2.42 to 2.34 ms and p95 3.30 to 3.37 ms. The longer comparison had mixed per-pair timings.
