prs.title: fix: a requested .opus CLI output no longer gets silently renamed to .ogg
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw infer tts convert --output ./voice.opus` (the voice-note example in the CLI docs) silently writes `./voice.ogg` instead. The output writer renames the file whenever the requested extension's MIME type doesn't match the sniffed MIME of the actual bytes, and sniffing an Ogg-contained Opus stream was always reporting the same generic `audio/ogg` as every other Ogg payload, so `.opus` could never match.

## User Impact

Running the documented voice-note example, or any CLI media command (`tts convert`, `image generate`, `video generate`) whose output lands as Ogg-contained Opus, now writes the file at the path the caller actually requested. A script that opens `./voice.opus` by that exact name no longer finds nothing. No action required; other mismatch detection (e.g. requesting `.mp3` and getting `.wav`) is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`file-type` already distinguishes Ogg-contained Opus from other Ogg payloads at the byte level (it reports `ext: "opus"` with a `codecs=opus` mime parameter, found only for the real `OpusHead` marker; Vorbis, FLAC and Speex all report a plain `audio/ogg`). `sniffMime()` in `packages/media-core/src/mime.ts` immediately ran that result through `normalizeMimeType()`, which strips mime parameters, throwing away the one piece of information that distinguished Opus from every other Ogg variant before any caller could use it.

The fix maps that specific, already-unambiguous case to this module's own existing canonical `audio/opus` MIME (the same value a `.opus` file extension already resolves to) at the one function that produces sniffed MIME values, rather than adding a special case in the CLI output writer. Every other Ogg payload is unaffected and still normalizes to `audio/ogg`.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test in `packages/media-core/src/mime.test.ts` using file-type's real `OggS` / `OpusHead` magic bytes (not mocked), proving `detectMime` now reports `audio/opus` for Opus-in-Ogg and still reports plain `audio/ogg` for Ogg Vorbis bytes.
- Added `src/cli/media-output.test.ts` (no prior test file existed for this module) exercising the actual `writeOutputAsset` CLI boundary end to end: a requested `.opus` output now keeps its `.opus` extension for real Opus-in-Ogg bytes, and a genuine mismatch (Ogg Vorbis bytes requested as `.opus`) still gets renamed to `.ogg`, confirming the existing mismatch-correction behavior is untouched.
- `pnpm vitest run src/cli/capability-cli.test.ts src/cli/media-output.test.ts packages/media-core/src/mime.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 235 passed, including the pre-existing `capability-cli.test.ts` case that pins the unrelated mp3-requested/wav-returned mismatch this same code path handles.
- `pnpm format:check`, oxlint, and `pnpm tsgo:core` on the touched files: clean.

Fixes #206612

prs.title: docs: warn that uninstalling a channel plugin deletes its channel settings
prs.body:
Closes #206927

## What Problem This Solves

When you uninstall a channel plugin, OpenClaw also deletes that channel's `channels.<channel-id>` settings: the account, allowlists and room config. The command's preview says so, but the Uninstall docs list what is removed and leave this out. Reinstalling doesn't restore the section, so someone who uninstalls and reinstalls to fix a problem loses their channel setup without the docs having warned them.

## User Impact

The Uninstall section now says that a channel plugin's `channels.<channel-id>` section is removed, how the preview names it, that `--keep-files` does not keep it, that reinstalling does not restore it, and to run `--dry-run` first and copy the section if you plan to reinstall. No behavior changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI is consistent and its preview is accurate, so this documents the current behavior instead of changing it. The paragraph sits right after the sentence that lists what uninstall removes, where a reader checks before running the command. Channel config was mentioned before only for the orphan-recovery case further down the section.

## Evidence

Reproduced on OpenClaw 2026.11.10 in an isolated state directory, with an XMPP channel plugin installed from a packed tarball:

- `openclaw config set channels.xmpp '{...}'`, then `openclaw config get channels.xmpp` printed the section.
- `openclaw plugins uninstall xmpp --dry-run` printed `Will remove: plugin settings, install record, channel config (channels.xmpp), directory: ...`.
- `openclaw plugins uninstall xmpp --force` printed `Uninstalled plugin "xmpp". Removed: plugin settings, install record, channel config, directory.`
- `openclaw config get channels.xmpp` then printed `Config path is valid but unset: channels.xmpp.`
- With `--keep-files`, the preview and result still listed `channel config (channels.xmpp)` and the section was unset afterwards.

That reinstalling does not restore the section was observed on 2026.11.9 (the gateway started without the channel after an uninstall and reinstall). I did not repeat the reinstall step on 2026.11.10, and I did not test a plugin that owns more than one channel.

Docs checks on this branch:

- `git diff --check`: clean
- `oxfmt@0.74.0 --check docs/cli/plugins/uninstall-and-update.md`: correct format
- `markdownlint-cli2 --config config/markdownlint-cli2.jsonc docs/cli/plugins/uninstall-and-update.md`: 0 issues

No links or headings were added.

prs.title: fix(agents): freeze every embedded dispatch and let harnesses declare who builds the prompt
prs.body:
## Problem

#206969 stopped a fallback model from failing a turn that an earlier model had already sent without a frozen model prompt (a "projection"). It did that by tolerating the missing projection for every harness. That tolerance also hid real gaps in the embedded runner, which is supposed to freeze every turn before sending it:

- An inter-session message (`sessions_send`) whose text was unchanged was sent without a projection. This is the case that failed a production turn.
- A turn that compaction removed from the request (a keyless turn) was sent without a projection.

## Fix

- Harnesses declare who builds the prompt with a new optional field, `promptProjection: "captures" | "external"`. The default is `"external"`, so undeclared third-party harnesses behave as before.
  - The built-in embedded harness declares `"captures"`. Codex declares `"external"`, because its app-server builds its own turn input.
  - The harness lifecycle records the declaration for one attempt only. The first send locks it in, and an attempt that never sent clears it.
- After a `"captures"` send, a late capture is an error again. The #206969 tolerance now applies only to `"external"` sends.
- The embedded runner makes that true. Unchanged inter-session text is now frozen too. Before the first send of an attempt, a turn that the prompt transform could not project is frozen as its own transcript text, so no fallback ever re-captures it.
- The new field is documented in `docs/plugins/sdk-agent-harness/core-ownership.md`.

## User impact

None visible on the normal path. A turn the embedded runner sends now always carries the text the provider received, so a later fallback on any harness replays the same bytes. Third-party harnesses that do not declare the field keep the current behavior.

## Evidence

- Red on main, green here:
  - The compacted keyless turn is frozen before dispatch, and the retained turn keeps no projection.
  - Inter-session turns are stored with their sent envelope (plain, forwarded and hook bodies).
- A built-in (`"captures"`) send without a projection makes a later capture throw; an undeclared harness keeps the tolerance.
- An attempt that never sent cannot apply its `"captures"` declaration to a later send outside the lifecycle.
- Projection and fallback suites on both routes pass: embedded submit, context and boundary, the recorder, the harness lifecycle, and the Codex app-server prompt projection.

prs.title: fix: shorten Doctor's Gateway outage spent checking for a running update
prs.body:
Related: #204775

## What Problem This Solves

While `openclaw doctor --fix` has the Gateway stopped, it checks before every state-database access that no `openclaw update` has started against the same state. On a healthy install that is about 6,500 checks per run. Most of them pay for a full read of the update ledger (about 1 ms each), and the ones made by steps that take their own SQLite lock, such as session transcript repair, start a `node` child process whenever Doctor's own writes have changed the database files. All of that is Gateway downtime spent finding nothing.

## User Impact

`doctor --fix` keeps the Gateway stopped for less time. The update check itself is unchanged: it still runs at every access, still sees committed rows only, and Doctor still refuses with the same message when an update run is active or appears while it is in maintenance. No config, schema, stored field or update-driver change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Doctor's admission reader keeps one independent read-only connection to the state database for its repair scope (#169905), so a check can query committed rows without a child process. Two things kept that cheap path from paying off:

1. **Nested step scopes were refused.** `withDoctorSqliteMaintenanceLock` (session transcripts, agent memory schema) takes a nested `sqlite-maintenance` owner, which opens a child maintenance scope inside Doctor's. The reader accepted only the exact scope it was bound to, so each of those accesses fell back to a private snapshot read, which starts a child process for the state content version whenever the files changed. A nested scope runs inside its parent's lifetime, so the reader now serves a scope whose ancestor it is bound to (the same `maintenanceResources.parents` chain that already lets nested scopes inherit the parent's live-read admission). It runs read admission for both the bound scope and the calling scope. Sibling and unrelated scopes still get fresh private reads.
2. **Every warm check re-read the ledger.** Each read repeats schema admission and the snapshot query, about 1 ms. The reader now reads SQLite's `PRAGMA data_version` on its own connection first, after its existing currency checks (scope admission, generation, file identity, quarantine). `data_version` changes exactly when another connection's commit becomes visible to this connection. If it is unchanged since just before the previous read, the previous rows are still exact and are returned; otherwise the reader reads again. The PRAGMA read lives in the SQLite PRAGMA owner (`sqlite-schema-catalog.ts`). PostgreSQL never reuses.

An earlier revision keyed reuse on the database file metadata instead. Review pointed out that SQLite writes WAL frames before it publishes the commit in the WAL index, so a read in that interval could cache pre-commit rows under post-commit metadata. `data_version` follows publication, so it has no such window.

**Invariant, from the code and the cells below.** Doctor must not touch state while an update run is active or pending. What an update does that Doctor would see is a `running` row in `update_runs`. While Doctor holds its maintenance owner, the update cannot write that row: every other OpenClaw process's state access is refused with "undergoing offline maintenance by sqlite-maintenance process …" (`assertPersistedStateDatabaseAccessAllowed`). The cells below start `openclaw update` during Doctor's session-transcript step: on `main` and on this branch it exits 1 about a second later and leaves no ledger table, and Doctor completes and restores the Gateway. The windows that stay open are before Doctor acquires its owner (service inspection and stop) and after it releases it (restoration). Those checks run outside the repair scope and are unchanged here. This change keeps every recheck inside maintenance; it only changes what each one costs.

**Not in this PR.** Checks outside a maintenance scope (service stop preparation and restoration) never retain a content-version revision, so each one still starts a child process: about 150 before the stop and 30 during restoration in the counts below (2.8 s of spawn time inside the stop under the counting preload). Open #201006 changes that owner to retain one revision per path, so this PR leaves it alone.

## Evidence

**Candidates.** Base `18e53d806db` (`main` when the branch was last cut). Tested head `4b8af744e24`; the PR head adds only a move of the one-line `data_version` read into the PRAGMA owner (`d5659ef0735`) and merges of `main` that do not touch the changed files or their callers. Both packed under the unpublished version 2026.11.13.

**Fixture.** Linux Docker container (systemd as PID 1, systemd user Gateway), npm global install of each pack, four agents with a 4.0 GiB main agent database, 1 MiB/s of writes into the other three agents while the Gateway serves, one seeded store restored byte-identical (sha256 over every file) before each run, no network for measured runs, `/healthz` probed every 250 ms, outage = time with no HTTP response. Section times come from Doctor's own trace.

**Outage, interleaved.** Six holds, one base/head pair each with one discarded warm-up per build, order alternating A,B / B,A. Host load (1-minute) 8 to 23 during the runs.

| | base `18e53d806db` median [range] | head median [range] |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway outage (no HTTP response) | 45.31 s [42.69-49.01] | 41.06 s [39.03-44.98] |
| Doctor "stopped for" | 47.90 s [44.80-52.00] | 43.75 s [42.00-47.60] |
| `doctor:session-transcripts` | 2.35 s [2.26-2.48] | 0.78 s [0.73-0.80] |
| `doctor.config-flow` | 6.44 s [6.08-6.81] | 5.14 s [4.81-5.39] |
| `doctor:agent-memory-schema` | 0.23 s [0.22-0.24] | 0.00 s [0.00-0.01] |
| `doctor:memory-search` | 1.37 s [1.33-1.52] | 1.27 s [1.20-1.38] |
| `doctor.maintenance.finish` (restoration, unchanged code) | 11.91 s [11.14-13.82] | 12.85 s [11.88-13.64] |

Paired outage differences (head minus base, per hold): -2.98, +0.51, -6.81, -5.12, -5.77, -5.61 s; median -5.37 s, head shorter in 5 of 6. Session-transcript step: -1.46 to -1.75 s in every pair. The restoration step ran a median 0.7 s longer on the head; this change does no work there (its checks run after Doctor releases its scope, through the unchanged cold path, with the same 30 child processes on both builds), so I read that as host noise, but it is not proven.

**Counts per `doctor --fix`** (one count run per build; counting preload and a copy of each build that marks every admission resolution):

| | base | head |
|---|---|---|
| admission resolutions inside the stop | 6,556 | 6,579 |
| of which in `doctor:session-transcripts` / config flow / backup | 4,387 / 1,004 / 363 | 4,387 / 1,004 / 386 |
| admission child processes inside the stop | 60 | 47 |
| in `doctor:session-transcripts` / `doctor:agent-memory-schema` | 12 / 2 | 0 / 0 |
| in restoration / maintenance begin / `doctor:memory-search` (outside the repair scope or before the backup boundary) | 30 / 12 / 4 | 30 / 12 / 5 |
| admission child processes before the stop | 149 | 153 |

Every access still resolves admission (the count is unchanged). What changed is the cost: no child process in nested steps, and about 0.06 ms instead of about 1 ms for a warm check while no other connection has committed (local measurement: base 1.03 ms per warm check and about 280 ms per check after a write in a nested step; head 0.06 ms and 1.8 ms).

**What the earlier 7.3 s estimate became.** The profile on #204775 put the recheck at 7.3 s of a healthy stop on an older build. On this build the measured part that this change can reach is about 3.2 s of section time (session transcripts 1.56, config flow 1.30, agent memory schema 0.23, memory search 0.10), and the outage medians differ by 4.25 s. What remains are the 47 child processes outside the repair scope (restoration 30, maintenance begin 12, memory search 5), which #201006 addresses.

**Update started during maintenance (invariant and negative control).** Same fixture with network, driver = the build under test, target = a 2026.11.14 pack served by a local registry. `openclaw update --yes --tag 2026.11.14` is started by an observed event: Doctor's trace line that `doctor:session-transcripts` began (Gateway inactive).

prs.title: fix: keep tool calls working in running agent turns after a tool-guard plugin reloads
prs.body:
Closes #205714

## What Problem This Solves

When you reload a plugin that checks tool calls (a `before_tool_call` guard) while an agent turn is running, every later tool call of that turn can be blocked with `Tool call blocked because before_tool_call hook failed` until the turn ends. Retrying inside the turn does not help, so the agent gives up or stops its task. It happens after a config edit the Gateway applied without a restart, the usual way people change settings.

## User Impact

Running turns keep their tools across a guard plugin reload: their next tool call goes through the reloaded guard, as the `Running turns on <id> continue on the new version at their next step` message promises. Nothing changes for turns that never see a reload. No action needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

After a hot config edit, a new run's config no longer matches the published plugin registry, so the run prepares its own registry that borrows the unchanged plugins from the Gateway's. A reload retires the Gateway registry but not the run's, and the hook runner keeps picking the run's registry. So it calls the disposed guard, and the refusal carries no replacement to retry.

The hook runner now uses the plugin's published successor for a borrowed record that can no longer admit calls, only when that successor is loaded. The hook takes the place the old registration held, and bundled tool policies stay first. A plugin the run loaded itself, one with `generationOverlap`, or one with no loaded successor keeps its own registration and still fails closed.

## Evidence

**Live, before and after:** fresh test Gateways with no model. A scripted CLI backend calls `session_status` over the MCP loopback 10 times, 1.5 s apart. Before the run, one hot config edit (`agents.defaults.modelPolicy.allow`). 5 s in, `openclaw plugins reload hook-probe`: a plugin with only a `before_tool_call` hook and `reload.turnHandover: true`.

| Build | Run | Tool calls ok | `before_tool_call hook failed` |
|---|---|---|---|
| main `6bdb5284285` | hot edit + reload, 4 runs (1 with a session model override) | 3, 2, 3, 2 of 10 | every call after `Plugin replacement applied` |
| main | hot edit, no reload | 10/10 | 0 |
| fix `2a02345e923` | hot edit + reload, 5 runs (1 with a session model override) | 10/10 each | 0; hook calls move to the new load mid-run |
| fix | hot edit, no reload | 10/10 | 0 |

Without the hot edit, main also passes: the run reuses the Gateway registry, which the reload retires. Instrumenting main's hook lookup showed the failing run's registry was not the published one but held the same `hook-probe` record.

![Gateway log: on main, 2/10 tool calls ok and every later call fails with PluginInstanceUnavailableError; on the fix, 10/10 and the reload applies](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stealthybear/openclaw/63b5432907a852222f86ce9f6d617e70f5411fc8/before-after.png)

Tested on `2a02345e923`.

- Review: autoreview (claude-fable-5) on `origin/main..2a02345e923`, all priorities: clean, "patch is correct".
- Test: `src/gateway/mcp-http.plugin-reload-hooks.test.ts` (new) reproduces the state in-process through the MCP loopback grant: fails on main, passes with the fix. 9.5 s (`pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1`).
- **No request proof:** the fix changes which hook registration runs, not what is sent to a model.

Not covered: embedded (non-CLI) runs were already fine on main (they hand over at a model step). A guard with `generationOverlap: true` keeps today's behavior.

prs.title: docs: explain why a loaded plugin tool is missing from the model's tool list
prs.body:
Closes #206915

## What Problem This Solves

If you write a tool plugin and install it, the plugin loads and `openclaw plugins inspect` lists the tool, but the tool isn't in the model's tool list and a model that calls it by name gets an error. The tool plugin guide has a "Tool does not appear after install" checklist, and every step on it passes, so the plugin looks broken when it is working as designed.

## User Impact

The checklist gets a sixth step. It says that embedded and Copilot runs use Tool Search when `tools.toolSearch` is unset, that the model reaches a plugin tool through `tool_search`, `tool_describe` and `dispatch_action`, how the call is shaped, and that `tools.toolSearch: false` gives direct schemas for checking. No behavior changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The behavior is already documented in `docs/tools/tool-search.md`. Plugin authors start from the tool plugin guide, which mentions Tool Search only in passing in two other sections, so the pointer belongs in the troubleshooting list they read when a tool seems missing. The step links to the Tool Search page instead of repeating it.

The wording follows `docs/tools/tool-search.md` on `main`: structured Tool Search is automatic for embedded and Copilot runs when `tools.toolSearch` is unset, `tools.toolSearch: false` restores direct schemas, and `dispatch_action` takes the tool `id` with target parameters under `args`.

## Evidence

Observed on OpenClaw 2026.11.9 with a one-tool `defineToolPlugin` plugin (`ntfy_notify`) in an embedded `openclaw agent --local` run against a stub OpenAI-compatible provider. I did not rerun this on current `main`.

- `openclaw plugins inspect ntfy --runtime --json` reported `status: loaded` with the tool under `toolNames`.
- The tools offered to the model were `apply_patch, dispatch_action, edit, exec, ls, message, openclaw, process, read, sessions_yield, tool_describe, tool_search, write`. The plugin tool was not among them.
- A model that called `ntfy_notify` directly got "OpenClaw stopped this turn: the same ntfy_notify call failed 3 times (unknown tool)."
- A model that called `tool_search` and then `dispatch_action` with `{ "id": "ntfy_notify", "args": { ... } }` ran the tool.

The test showing the working flow: https://github.com/rickysinghmba/openclaw-ntfy/blob/main/test/e2e.test.js

Docs checks on this branch:

- `git diff --check`: clean
- `oxfmt@0.74.0 --check docs/plugins/tool-plugins.md`: correct format
- `markdownlint-cli2 --config config/markdownlint-cli2.jsonc docs/plugins/tool-plugins.md`: 0 issues

The step adds one link, to `/tools/tool-search`, which the same page already links to. I did not run the docs link audit.

prs.title: fix(matrix): report media presentation duration
prs.body:
# fix(matrix): report media presentation duration

## Two changes

1. **Remove the redundant AIFC/IMA4 correction.** music-metadata 12.3.1 fixed Apple’s IMA4 packet-count interpretation upstream. Matrix already declares 12.3.2, which includes the fix. The recipient received a 640 ms duration for a clip that FFmpeg independently decoded to 28,224 mono frames at 44,100 Hz. [Upstream AIFC fix](https://github.com/Borewit/music-metadata/pull/2869)
2. **Use the container’s playback duration for all audio and video attachments.** PR #205285 correctly switched edited single-track AAC to the movie timeline. Its codec and track-count guards left other attachments using the media duration even when the parser supplied the whole presentation duration. Prefer `containerDuration` whenever present and fall back to `duration`.

## Evidence

### Live Matrix send and recipient readback at `21a1c70840a`

Built the exact PR head in a detached checkout with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` and verified the Matrix plugin resolved music-metadata **12.3.2**. Ran `pnpm openclaw message send --channel matrix --target <room> --media <fixture> --json` against isolated **Synapse 1.163.2**. A separate account fetched each persisted `m.room.message` and downloaded each attachment through the authenticated Matrix media API. Every download matched the input byte for byte.

| Playable fixture | Recipient event | `info.duration` at the PR head |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| MP4 with two AAC tracks | `m.audio` | 800 ms |
| WebM with VP9 and Opus, Segment Duration present | `m.video` | 800 ms |
| Matroska with VP9 and Opus, Segment Duration present | `m.video` | 800 ms |
| WebM and Matroska produced in live muxing mode, Segment Duration absent | `m.video` | Omitted for both |
| AIFC/IMA4, 28,224 decoded mono samples at 44,100 Hz | `m.audio` | 640 ms |

**Before and after on the same playable AAC file.** With the same built CLI, homeserver, and pinned parser, loading the previous Matrix plugin source from `63876e38367` produced **521 ms**. The PR head produced **800 ms**, matching ffprobe’s container timeline. Both recipient downloads had SHA-256 `71263ea4ed8907d4aecde3c5c84be0848b24308a3288ffeeb421e4fa3b38fc4c`.

**Video scope.** The pinned parser returned 800 ms in both duration fields for the ordinary WebM and Matroska clips. For the live-muxed clips it returned neither field, and both events still arrived with intact attachments and duration omitted. The real AAC comparison demonstrates the changed choice when the two fields differ.

### AIFC and IMA4

The following live evidence comes from the earlier AIFC-only implementation.

On 2026-10-25, ran the shipped `pnpm openclaw message send` CLI from head `a97a2b1670c3e821ecc7ab7da1afda32f1ad755b`, using Matrix's installed music-metadata **12.3.1**, against a real isolated **Synapse 1.163.2** homeserver. Separate temporary sender and recipient accounts joined a private, unencrypted room. No sender, parser, SDK, upload, transport, or homeserver response was mocked.

Redacted terminal/recipient output:

```text
$ pnpm openclaw message send --channel matrix --target <redacted-room> --media <fixture>/ima4-640ms.aifc --json
CLI: deliveryStatus=sent; remote echo received
Recipient: GET room event returned m.room.message
Recipient content: {"msgtype":"m.audio","info":{"duration":640,"mimetype":"audio/aiff","size":15098},"url":"<redacted-mxc>"}
Recipient download: 15098 bytes; identical to original clip
SHA-256: b66be0f0a41e508612a89b84b8b60b8cb410fdd569a1f4d6e7f8873f7383c002
Independent FFmpeg decode: 28224 mono frames / 44100 Hz = 640 ms
```

This exercises the shipped CLI send route and verifies the persisted event and attachment using the recipient's token. The homeserver was local and isolated; no external production homeserver delivery is claimed. The CLI printed its successful delivery receipt but remained running afterward; its task-owned process was terminated after recipient verification. Temporary accounts, credentials and server state were removed with the isolated server.

### AAC, WebM, and Matroska

Generated a playable MP4 with two AAC-LC sine tracks at 48 kHz, lasting 500 ms and 800 ms. FFmpeg decoded both streams. The same file went through the real Matrix sender and music-metadata 12.3.3 on the previous AIFC-only commit and the current change, with a synthetic media source and Matrix client. Both captures checked that the upload received the original bytes.

```text
$ ffmpeg -hide_banner -i two-track.m4a -map 0:a -f null -
Duration: 00:00:00.80, start: 0.000000, bitrate: 138 kb/s
Stream #0:0 -> #0:0 (aac (native) -> pcm_s16le (native))
Stream #0:1 -> #0:1 (aac (native) -> pcm_s16le (native))
size=N/A time=00:00:00.80

$ ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration:stream=codec_name,duration -of compact two-track.m4a
stream|codec_name=aac|duration=0.500000
stream|codec_name=aac|duration=0.800000
format|duration=0.800000

Matrix event info before: {"size":13854,"mimetype":"audio/mp4","duration":521}
Matrix event info after:  {"size":13854,"mimetype":"audio/mp4","duration":800}
```

Matrix writes the selected duration to `info.duration` for audio and video and to `org.matrix.msc1767.audio.duration` for voice messages.

| Attachment | Audio media duration | Container presentation duration | Matrix event duration |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Edited single-track AAC, sent as audio and voice | 555 ms | 500 ms | 500 ms |
| Edited two-track AAC | 555 ms | 525 ms | 525 ms |
| Unedited AAC | 299 ms | 299 ms | 299 ms |
| WebM video | 40 ms | 100 ms | 100 ms |
| Matroska video | 40 ms | 100 ms | 100 ms |

The AAC cases use the real parser. With the previous single-track AAC condition, Matrix reported 555 ms for the two-track file.

The WebM and Matroska cases supply both durations through stubbed parser metadata and observe the Matrix video event. The same timing distinction was reproduced with EBML fixtures in the music-metadata 13.0.2 checkout. OpenClaw’s installed music-metadata 12.3.3 did not derive durations from those fixtures, which omit Segment Duration. The Matrix evidence covers selection when the parser supplies the values.

### Playable WebM and Matroska files

Generated both containers with VP9 video and Opus audio using FFmpeg’s live muxing mode, which omits Segment Duration. FFmpeg decoded both streams in both files with `-xerror`. The same command works with either extension.

```sh
ffmpeg -v error \
  -f lavfi -i color=size=32x32:rate=25:duration=0.8 \
  -f lavfi -i sine=sample_rate=48000:duration=0.5 \
  -c:v libvpx-vp9 -c:a libopus -live 1 clip.webm
ffmpeg -v error -xerror -i clip.webm -map 0:v -map 0:a -f null -
```

| File | ffprobe last video packet end | ffprobe last audio packet end | music-metadata 13.0.2 `duration` | music-metadata 13.0.2 `containerDuration` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `clip.webm` | 0.800 s | 0.501 s | 0.4945 s | 0.800 s |
| `clip.mkv` | 0.800 s | 0.501 s | 0.4945 s | 0.800 s |

The ffprobe columns use the maximum packet timestamp plus packet duration for each stream. The parser’s audio value accounts for Opus codec delay. With the older music-metadata 12.3.3 installed in the OpenClaw checkout, both duration fields were absent for these playable files as well. The playable files demonstrate the parser-level distinction. The separate Matrix sender regressions demonstrate the event’s duration selection when metadata provides both values.

Supersedes #183516

prs.title: fix: distinguish filenames with spaces in cron stream schedules
prs.body:
Closes #206894

## What Problem This Solves

When inspecting a stream automation, you couldn't tell whether it read one file named `a b` or two files named `a` and `b`. Both schedules appeared as `stream cat a b` in `cron show` and `cron list`.

## User Impact

Stream schedules with spaces, quotes, or other special characters now show the argument array accepted by `--stream-command`. Simple commands still fit the compact text view. This changes how the CLI displays a saved schedule.

## Why This Change Was Made

Joining arguments with spaces loses the boundaries that the scheduler stores. Both text views use the same schedule formatter, which can print the original array as JSON when the compact form would be ambiguous.

## Evidence

I built the CLI before and after the change and ran each build against a fresh loopback Gateway with scheduling disabled. I created two disabled jobs and read each job back through `cron show`, `cron show --json`, and `cron list --all`.

| Saved argument array | Previous schedule line | New schedule line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `["cat","a b"]` | `stream cat a b` | `stream ["cat","a b"]` |
| `["cat","a","b"]` | `stream cat a b` | `stream cat a b` |

The list showed the same distinction. Both builds returned the original argument arrays in JSON. The regression failed on the base commit and passed with the fix. All 198 tests in the cron rendering, Gateway pagination, and trigger-option suites passed, including coverage for quotes, backslashes, and a newline in an argument.

The two acceptance commands from #206894 also passed (111 cron CLI tests and 14 argument-quoting tests).

prs.title: feat: find Knowledge notes across word boundaries and word forms
prs.body:
Related: #206610, #205667. Related implementations: #206642 and #205754.

## What Problem This Solves

A Knowledge note can contain the answer and still be invisible to keyword search. A Portuguese query for `combinar` misses a note saying `combinámos`; a Japanese query for `東京` misses `明日東京で会います` when the sentence is indexed as one token.

## User Impact

This draft makes those examples searchable without rewriting Markdown, citations or snippet offsets. An omitted-mode query first requires every literal term, including in eligible superseded wording. Only after a miss can it strip a recognized English or Portuguese question prefix **or** try a narrow set of whole-word inflections. It never does both, never silently switches to any-word search, and reports the adjustment as `matchStrategy`. Explicit `all`, `any`, and `phrase` keep their literal strategies.

**Not recommended for merge as implemented.** On 128 mixed-language notes, median warm hit latency went from **0.82 to 16.19 ms**. There is no persistent index migration, new dependency, configuration change, embedding, or change to passive recall.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing scoped FTS/BM25 search ranks the same eligible records. The prototype gives it ICU dictionary word boundaries in a query-local index and retains significant Thai, Lao, Khmer and kana marks. It does not apply English Porter stemming across languages, treat every CJK substring as a word, or interpret either proposed `keyword_fts_v2` format as the other.

**Decision requested:** should Knowledge match dictionary words or arbitrary CJK substrings? Which directional inflections and adjustment disclosure should be part of the public search contract? If those semantics are accepted, a single versioned projection built during reconciliation needs its own design and migration review. This draft does not choose a durable format or retire v1.

## Evidence

- **Shared `memory.search` disclosure (ClawSweeper P2):** Before the fix, `where is orchid` returned the saved orchid note but its `warning` mentioned only coverage. The provider now reports when it omitted the question prefix or used alternate word forms (`combinar` / `combinámos`), alongside the original coverage notice. A literal `orchid` search still has no adjustment notice. The regression ran through the real provider and SQLite vault; `pnpm test extensions/knowledge/src/memory-provider.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` passed all 17 tests. This does not change the persistent index, shared API schema or the design hold.

| Labeled query–record pairs | Base `1decc861a62c` | Draft | Extra records, base → draft |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Original corpus: 14 notes, 27 queries | 6/20 | 17/20 | 1 → 1 |
| Held-out corpus: 6 notes, 35 queries | 2/18 | 16/18 | 0 → 0 |

On the original corpus, the draft recovered `reunião`, `decisão`, `combinar`, and `서울` before a particle, among other terms. It still missed French `billet` and the Khmer fragment `ភាសា` in a dictionary compound. It deliberately declined `orchid zephyrium` rather than also treating `orchid refunds` as a match for an orchid-only note. The one extra record contains the Portuguese word `Nas`, a literal case-insensitive match for `NAS`. A word form is not a sense judgment: noun-intended `jantar` can match the verb `jantámos`. These synthetic judgments are not a general precision estimate.

- The same fixed fixture checked actual service results, source SHA-256s and snippet slices on both versions. A separate registered-tool flow saved a page into an isolated vault, searched from agent and operator surfaces, and read it back. No live store or live Gateway/model turn was used.
- `pnpm test extensions/knowledge/src/retrieval.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: **24 passed**, including original offsets, Thai rice/news, scope and withdrawals, strict modes, Portuguese past tense, and literal history precedence before pagination. Production package-boundary compile, type-only checking of Knowledge sources, targeted lint/format, and diff checks passed locally. Review caught meaningful Thai marks, double widening of question terms, and an NFC-only form that missed decomposed Korean. The NFD regression returned `[]` before the fix and the expected record afterward. Final independent static review reported no P0–P2 findings. Local checks are not hosted CI or a ClawSweeper rating.
- Paired retrieval-kernel benchmark (Node 24.20.0, ICU 78.3, SQLite 3.53.4; 209,856 UTF-8 body bytes; 12 alternating warm samples per query per version): hit **0.82 → 16.19 ms**, miss **0.52 → 15.64 ms**, TEMP high-water allocation **0 → 331,776 bytes**. After the canonical-form repair the same benchmark measured **0.69 → 16.16 ms** for a warm hit. These are retrieval-kernel timings, not end-to-end user latency or production-scale costs.

## Worked on by

- @TheAngryPit

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

prs.title: fix(doctor): skip the state schema repair when its read-only plan finds nothing
prs.body:
Related: #204775

## What Problem This Solves

Every `openclaw doctor --fix` stops the Gateway and, inside that stop, runs the shared state database's schema repair, even on a healthy install where it changes nothing. On a healthy Linux install it opens the state database, the local credential store and the quarantine store for writing, takes the schema lease, starts three write transactions, runs 12 write statements that change no row, and invalidates the clean-close seal. Doctor mode has repaired unconditionally since #155446 because nothing could prove the repair had no work. This is one of the unconditional pieces that keep Doctor from skipping the stop when nothing needs repair.

## User Impact

On a healthy install, `doctor --fix` no longer opens any store for writing or takes the schema lease for this repair. When any condition the repair acts on is present, or the plan cannot decide, the repair runs exactly as before. Doctor still stops the Gateway and runs every step; the `config-flow` step's own pending answer stays `work`. No schema, stored field, config option or permission changes. No operator action.

## Why This Change Was Made

`planOpenClawStateDatabaseDoctorRepair` (`src/state/openclaw-state-db-doctor-repair-plan.ts`) lists every condition the doctor-scope repair acts on for a store at the current schema version, taken from the repair's code write by write. Each condition is decided at the owner of the step that writes, from the same rows or catalog entries that step changes. Where a writer had no read-only check, its planning moved into a shared function that both the writer and the check use, so the two cannot drift:

| Condition | What the repair does (`openclaw-state-db-repair.ts` unless noted) | Read-only decision | Guard fixture (unit, real store) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `permissions` | `ensureOpenClawStatePermissions` before and after (241, 677) | `hasOpenClawStatePermissionDrift`, before any open | database file at 0644 |
| `recorded-damage` | index rescan, full integrity check and quarantine clear (383–433, 629) | `hasRecordedStateDatabaseDamage` | persisted quarantine verdict |
| `catalog-readability` | readability repair of the dangling review index (260–278, 625) | `hasDanglingSkillWorkshopCollectionReviewIndex` | dangling Skill Workshop index |
| `registry-key` | refuses: `assertCanonicalAgentDatabasesPrimaryKey` (237) | same assertion | registry rebuilt with another key (refusal) |
| `schema-version` | `normalizeSqliteText`, bounded migrations, `markCurrentStateSchemaVersion` (279–295, 507–520, 605) | header, content-version row and `schema_meta` (`hasCurrentStateSchemaVersionWork`, `openclaw-state-schema-publication.ts`) | `schema_meta` one version behind |
| `integrity` | index scan or orphan recovery after `classifyStateDatabaseIntegrity` (386–405, 503) | the same quick or full check, run fresh | damaged index key (full check) |
| `quarantine-store` | `clearOpenClawDatabaseQuarantine` (629) | `hasOpenClawDatabaseQuarantineClearWork` (`openclaw-quarantine-store.ts`) | schema-1 store; store whose clear fails (refusal) |
| `orphan-task-delivery` | `recoverOrphanTaskDeliveryRows` (462–473, 502) | `hasOrphanTaskDeliveryRows` | delivery row without its task |
| `client-credentials` | custody open and `recoverClientCredentialStore` (296–315, 523) | `hasClientCredentialStoreRecoveryWork`: custody checks read-only, then the same receipt decision (`client-credential-recovery-plan.ts`) | receipt left in the `copied` phase |
| `historical-image-snapshots` | `migrateHistoricalStateImports(…, "doctor")` (506) | `hasHistoricalImageReserveSnapshots` | reserve snapshot with a retired image project |
| `required-tables` | refuses: `assertSqliteSchemaTablesPresent` (531) | same assertion | `subagent_runs` dropped (refusal) |
| `legacy-tables` | `dropLegacyStateTables` (535) | `LEGACY_STATE_TABLES` present | `node_pairing_pending` created |
| `audit-and-approval-schema` | `repairAuditEventsSchema`, `repairOperatorApprovalSchema`, `assertCanonicalStateSchemaShape` (546–560) | `hasCanonicalAuditEventsSchema`, `detectOperatorApprovalSchemaMigration`, same assertion | operator approvals in the two-kind legacy layout |
| `session-watch` | `migrateSessionWatchCursorProvenance` (552–559) | `needsSessionWatchCursorProvenanceMigration` | legacy ambient-watch sentinel row |
| `publication-drafts` | `statePublicationDraftMigration`, the one versioned migration that is not version-gated (571) | `needsPublicationDraftMigration` | publication table without its `draft` column |
| `additive-schema` | `ensureAdditiveStateColumns(…, "repair")` catalog changes (570) | `hasAdditiveStateSchemaRepairWork` (`openclaw-state-db-schema-additive.ts`) | retired diagnostic index created |
| `acp-replay-accounting` | `backfillAcpReplayEstimatedBytes` (570) | `hasAcpReplayEstimatedBytesWork` | completion record deleted |
| `cron-job-projection` | `backfillCronJobsFromJobJson` (570) | `hasCronJobProjectionWork`, shared planner (new) | job with a stale projection |
| `delivery-queue` | `backfillDeliveryQueueEntriesFromEntryJson`: failure compaction, receipt pruning, projection (570) | `hasDeliveryQueueBackfillWork`, shared planners (new; no read-only check existed) | pending row with a lagging retry count; completed receipt past retention |
| `subagent-runs` | `repairLegacySubagentExecutionPayloads`, `repairLegacySubagentRetainedResults` (570) | shared `WHERE` clause and shared rewrite planner | run with root terminal fields |
| `operator-approval-refs` | `ensureOperatorApprovalResolutionRefs` (570) | `hasOperatorApprovalResolutionRefWork`, shared planner | reference index dropped |
| `legacy-cron-run-logs` | `backfillCronRunLogEntryJson`, `migrateLegacyCronRunLogsToTaskRuns` (570, 580) | `hasLegacyCronRunLogs` | retired `cron_run_logs` table |
| `canonical-catalog` | `executeCanonicalStateSchema` and the STRICT rebuild (576–597) | every runtime table present and STRICT, no schema issue against the canonical SQL | runtime table rebuilt without STRICT (refusal) |
| `canonical-indexes` | `repairCanonicalSqliteIndexes` (598) | `hasCanonicalSqliteIndexRepairs`, shared comparison (`sqlite-index-schema.ts`) | canonical index with another definition |
| `runtime-schema` | refuses before commit: `assertCurrentStateRuntimeSchema` (609) | same assertion | covered by the catalog fixtures |

The version-gated steps (text normalization, bounded and historical migrations, table retirements, the v8, v9, v12 and v21 repairs, and every versioned migration except publication drafts) act only below the current version, which `schema-version` decides.

#155446 made doctor mode repair unconditionally so that every run gets a fresh integrity check and its later full repair. The plan keeps both: it runs the same quick or full integrity check the repair would run, on the live file, at the time of the run, and reuses no earlier result. Anything it cannot decide, including a read error, answers `undecidable`, and the repair runs.

The plan reads the live stores through `decideDoctorPendingFromLiveStores` (#206485): a store nobody holds open is `undecidable`, as is an updater's capture or PostgreSQL. It opens the state, credential and quarantine stores read-only, never copies, takes no lease and starts no write transaction. Permission drift is decided before any open, because a read-only open of a store whose file mode drifted re-modes its WAL.

`prepareOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema` in doctor mode consumes the plan: `none` returns before the lease, the write-mode open and the cached-handle close; anything else repairs as before. The repair itself is unchanged.

The `config-flow` pending check now lists its inputs explicitly (`src/commands/doctor-config-flow-pending.ts`): the state schema plan, traced as `doctor.pending.config-flow.state-schema`, plus the agent database migration and the plugin obligation ledger, which have no predicate yet and keep the step at `work`. Adding either later is one `check` there.

This builds on its own read of the credential store's receipt and does not touch the custody open that #206513 changes, so the two land in either order.

## Evidence

Tested commit for the cells below: `39099fae3bb` (this branch with `main` merged). After it: a merge of `main` (no change to the touched owners or callers), test fixtures for the remaining conditions, the same schema-version query rewritten through Kysely (`ea4c2aa27e8`), and the plan module loaded lazily by Doctor only, listed in the PR wrapper inventory (`b4f662b89aa`). Unit tests cover all of these at `b4f662b89aa`, and the green cell was rerun on a pack of that exact head (same fixture and steps): both `doctor --fix` runs traced `config-flow.state-schema` `none` (79 / 78 ms), with 0 write-mode opens, 0 `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` and no lease from the state schema owner (10 ms in the graph).

**Red on unmodified `main` (`39b6a89d298`), through the real CLI.** Linux container, systemd user Gateway, npm install of a locally built pack, healthy install. Two `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_STARTUP_TRACE=1 openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive --yes` runs under an io-trace preload that records every write-mode SQLite open, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, write statement and write-intent file call. Inside the legacy state migration graph, the state schema repair (events from its first to its last call) did, in each run:

| | base `39b6a89d298` | head `39099fae3bb` |
|---|---|---|
| write-mode opens (state, credential, quarantine stores) | 3 | 0 |
| `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` | 3 | 0 |
| write statements that changed no row | 12 | 0 |
| rows changed | 0 | 0 |
| schema lease taken | 1 | 0 |
| clean-close seal unlinks | 2 | 0 |
| time in the state schema owner | 86 / 88 ms | 16 / 14 ms (the plan) |
| `doctor.pending.config-flow.state-schema` | (no input) | `none`, 102 / 93 ms |
| `doctor.pending.config-flow` | `work check=default` | `work check=owner` |

Red recording (raw log replay, base):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bff9562c-cb24-4cb6-a1a8-998842a0f63f

Green recording (same fixture, steps and observation point, head):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6997c88f-9f66-4eb3-8b51-a9572ca87ea9

The `config-flow.state-schema` check costs about 0.1 s inside the stop, most of it the first import of the plan module, while the skipped repair saved about 0.07 s in the graph. Until checks run before the stop, the stopped time does not shrink from this change; see the interleaved timing below.

**Guards through the real CLI** (same cell shape, base `39b6a89d298` and head `39099fae3bb`). Each condition was really created with the Gateway stopped, the Gateway restarted, then `doctor --fix` ran twice under the io trace. Repaired rows were dumped after the first run and compared between base and head.

| Condition seeded | head plan, 1st run | head repair, 1st run | head plan, 2nd run | repaired content vs base |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `node_pairing_pending` table (`legacy-tables`) | `work` | ran (3 write-mode opens) | `none`, 0 opens | identical (table dropped) |
| pending delivery row with lagging retry count (`delivery-queue`) | `work` | ran | `none`, 0 opens | identical (`retry_count` 2, channel set) |
| cron job with stale projection (`cron-job-projection`) | `work` | ran | `none`, 0 opens | identical (name and payload kind projected) |
| ACP recount record deleted (`acp-replay-accounting`) | `work` | ran | `none`, 0 opens | identical (record restored) |
| `schema_meta` one version behind (`schema-version`) | `work` | already fixed earlier in the same run by the config preflight's schema preparation; the graph's repair then found nothing (0 opens) | `none` | identical (version 42) |
| receipt phase `copied` (`client-credentials`) | `none` | not needed | `none` | identical (`complete`) |
| state file mode 0644 (`permissions`) | `none` | not needed | `none` | identical (0600) |

For the last two, the state was already restored before the config flow ran, on base and head alike (by the Gateway's restart or an earlier Doctor step; the trace does not attribute it), so in a real run the plan met them fixed. Their plan conditions are proven by the unit fixtures, where the plan sees them. Base ran the repair, with its 3 write-mode opens, in every one of these 14 runs.

<details><summary>Raw guard comparison (home paths shortened)</summary>

```
=== GUARDS: each condition really created while the Gateway was stopped, then doctor --fix twice
base pack 2026.11.27 39b6a89d298, head pack 2026.11.29 39099fae3bb; Linux, systemd user Gateway, npm

## legacy-tables
  base work: plan n/a (base has no plan); write-mode opens by the repair: 3
  base again: plan n/a (base has no plan); write-mode opens by the repair: 3
  base result: { "condition": "legacy-tables", "rows": [], "stateMode": "600"}

  head again: plan pending=none; write-mode opens by the repair: 0

## schema-version
```

prs.title: improve(discord): guide Goal actions with native subcommands
prs.body:
Related: #205931

## What Problem This Solves

Discord's `/goal` command uses separate `action` and `text` fields, leaving users to work out which text each action needs. Checking a goal and starting one look like the same form, despite needing different inputs.

## User Impact

The command picker guides users through eight subcommands:
- `start` and `edit`: required `objective`.
- `pause`, `resume`, `complete`, and `block`: optional `note`.
- `status` and `clear`: no additional fields.

The new form appears after Discord command registration refreshes. Text-based `/goal` commands, other channels, and Goal execution are unchanged. No production bot registration was changed. This PR remains draft while publicly inspectable visual proof is missing.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use Discord's existing subcommand support to make each action's inputs explicit. The adapter translates those inputs into the existing Goal arguments, preserving shared authorization, session routing, and Goal execution. No dependency, config, or state-schema changes.

Rollback is to revert the adapter change and refresh Discord command registration.

## Evidence

- **Automated:** the two affected suites pass (29 tests total, 19.57s local wall time). New Goal coverage is limited to one serialized-registration contract and four representative dispatch cases: objective, optional note supplied/omitted, and field-free status. Existing shared authorization tests are reused. Focused test typechecking, lint, formatting, and whitespace checks pass. Independent scoped autoreview completed clean; this is not an exhaustive review. The published tree matches the tested candidate `6297470755ce7889f60c6293fbe165b4a4dc8c79`. Hosted CI for the new head is not yet verified.
- **Live Discord:** human-triggered native start/status behavior and client-visible outputs were observed on the unchanged production implementation. Correlated runtime state recorded three automatic continuations, `status: complete`, and no active run. [Sanitized runtime evidence](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/205976#issuecomment-7195090994).
- **Picker captures:** human-supplied before/after captures have been inspected locally: the old flat form, objective entry, optional note picker, and field-free clear are captured. An omission attempt enforcing required objective was not exercised. Sanitized public embedding remains blocked; these private captures are not presented as public visual proof.
- **Review:** ClawSweeper's earlier review of `0ae21bb92286106b74fe8639ad20c21e0a4d242c` found no actionable code defects but remained blocked on public picker proof and maintainer approval of the layout. That verdict does not cover the new head. No new re-review request is claimed.
- **Remaining gaps:** publicly inspectable before/after picker images, exhaustive lifecycle execution, broad hosted build/test CI, and maintainer acceptance of the native layout. Earlier upstream attachment upload required repository write access; public-fork asset URLs returned HTTP 404.

This update changes tests only: representative dispatch coverage replaces per-action replays, and registration checks include String field types. Production code is unchanged from the previously published head; no rebase was performed.

prs.title: fix: report failing OAuth stage and request ID when ChatGPT sign-in returns an HTTP error
prs.body:
Related: #204662

## What Problem This Solves

When Sign in with ChatGPT (`models.authLogin` / `openclaw models auth login --provider openai --method siwc`) or a subsequent token refresh fails with a server-side HTTP error such as `HTTP 403`, OpenClaw reports only `ChatGPT authentication request failed (HTTP 403). Retry sign-in later.` (for login/JWKS) or `ChatGPT token-sharing refresh failed (403): provider_error` (for refresh) without saying which server-side OAuth stage failed or surfacing any upstream request identifier. That leaves users and maintainers unable to tell which endpoint rejected the request or correlate the failure with upstream support logs.

## User Impact

When a ChatGPT sign-in, JWKS fetch, or token refresh request returns a non-2xx HTTP status (other than `invalid_grant`, whose reconnect message is preserved unchanged), the error message now includes bounded, sanitized diagnostics:

- **Token exchange HTTP 403**:
  - Before: `ChatGPT authentication request failed (HTTP 403). Retry sign-in later.`
  - After: `ChatGPT authentication request failed during token exchange (HTTP 403, access_denied, x-request-id=req_403_trace_01). Retry sign-in later.`
- **Signing key (`jwks.json`) fetch HTTP 403**:
  - Before: `ChatGPT authentication request failed (HTTP 403). Retry sign-in later.`
  - After: `ChatGPT authentication request failed during signing key fetch (HTTP 403, cf-ray=8f1234567890-SJC). Retry sign-in later.`
- **Token refresh HTTP 403** (preserving `oauthRefreshOutcome` and `invalid_grant` handling):
  - Before: `ChatGPT token-sharing refresh failed (403): provider_error`
  - After: `ChatGPT token-sharing refresh failed (403): provider_error (x-request-id=req_403_trace_01)`

Raw provider response bodies and credentials are never exposed, and malformed request-ID headers containing whitespace or control characters are ignored. No user action or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

`requestJson` in `extensions/openai/token-sharing-oauth.runtime.ts` already enforces bounded response reading and intentionally omits provider response bodies to prevent credential leakage. Passing an explicit `OAuthRequestStage` label from its three call sites (`token exchange`, `token refresh`, `signing key fetch`), enriching both the `refresh_token` error branch (without altering `oauthRefreshOutcome` or `invalid_grant` recovery semantics) and the general non-2xx login/JWKS branch, and extracting only strictly validated single-token identifiers (`^[A-Za-z0-9_.:/-]{1,128}$`) closes the diagnostic gap noted in `#204662` across all three OAuth stages.

## Evidence

Verified on Node `v24.22.3` (commit `565a1d3b1`):

1. **Base (`origin/main`) fails on all 4 new regression tests**:
   ```text
   $ pnpm vitest run extensions/openai/token-sharing-oauth.runtime.test.ts -t 'reports OAuth stage|reports signing key fetch|reports bounded upstream request ID|ignores malformed request ID'
   × reports OAuth stage and bounded upstream request ID on HTTP 403 without leaking body text
   × reports signing key fetch stage and cf-ray when JWKS returns HTTP 403
   × reports bounded upstream request ID on refresh HTTP 403 while preserving refresh outcome
   × ignores malformed request ID headers containing whitespace or control characters
   Test Files  1 failed (1)
        Tests  4 failed | 35 skipped (39)
   ```
2. **Fix (`565a1d3b1`) passes all 39 tests**:
   ```text
   $ pnpm vitest run extensions/openai/token-sharing-oauth.runtime.test.ts
   Test Files  1 passed (1)
        Tests  39 passed (39)
   ```
   (These tests exercise the real local loopback OAuth callback server in `loginTokenSharing` and `refreshTokenSharingCredential` with stubbed `auth.openai.com` HTTP responses; live `auth.openai.com` 403 reproduction was not run because it requires an affected ChatGPT account.)
3. **Lint & format**:
   - `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/openai/token-sharing-oauth.runtime.ts extensions/openai/token-sharing-oauth.runtime.test.ts` — `Found 0 warnings and 0 errors.`
   - `pnpm exec oxfmt --check extensions/openai/token-sharing-oauth.runtime.ts extensions/openai/token-sharing-oauth.runtime.test.ts` — `All matched files use the correct format.`

prs.title: fix(sessions): clear stale compactionQualityDegraded on rewind/branch switch
prs.body:
Fixes #204060

## What Problem This Solves
After a lossy compaction, `compactionQualityDegraded: true` is written to the session entry. Rewinding to before that turn (or switching branches) cleared `compactionCount` but not the degraded flag, so `/status` kept showing `Compactions: 0 · degraded history (details may be lost)` even though the context was fully restored — a false "degraded" warning on a healthy session.

## Change
`buildMessageCutSessionEntry` now derives the degradation flag from the selected transcript path on every rewind / branch-switch / fork commit: the flag is cleared when the new path contains no quality-degraded compaction, and kept (recomputed from the active path's compaction events) when it does. No change to the status formatter's zero-count warning logic, and no unconditional clearing — switching back to a still-degraded history restores the warning.

Also fixed while testing: fork planning only saw navigation-projected compaction rows (no `details`), so the planner could not see degradation info; the fork read path now exposes `hasDegradedCompaction(prefix)`, which reads only the selected prefix's compaction payloads one at a time instead of hydrating every summary.

## Evidence
- 5 new regression tests: SQLite (rewind clears, switch away/back restores, fork prefix) and memory (rewind clears, switch away/back restores).
- SQLite message-cut file: 17/17 passed; memory fork file: 8/8 passed; `sessions-rewind` (+incognito): 30/30; `status-message`: 28/28.
- Failing-first verified for the rewind + switch SQLite tests (failed on base with "expected true to be undefined", green with the fix).
- Rebased onto current upstream main (b647c1be) and re-ran both targeted suites after the rebase: 17/17 and 8/8 green.
- Not verified locally: `pnpm tsgo:core` (typecheck) could not run on my machine (OOM; the repo's own docs note tsgo peaks at ~8.4 GiB). Please let CI run it. The fork test was not run red-on-base separately (its red state follows directly from the base code never setting the flag).

### Update: ClawSweeper rework (2026-11-24)

Both P2 regressions are fixed; the flag-derivation behavior is unchanged (rewind clears, switching back to degraded history restores).

**Fork read budget.** `readSessionMessageCut` no longer hydrates every compaction payload before the planner picks the prefix. The read result now exposes `hasDegradedCompaction(prefix)`, which reads only the selected prefix's compaction payloads one at a time (per-event budget guard, no retention, no charge to the cumulative 8 MiB navigation budget). This preserves the streaming intent of b62210f: only navigation, header, and editor data stay resident while copied payloads stream.

**Ordinary rewind scan.** `selectedPathHasDegradedCompaction` now fast-paths via the active-path projection for targets on the active path with no reset after them (compaction seqs from `session_transcript_active_events` up to the target position, payload reads one at a time; `targetId === null` returns false immediately). Canonical tree resolution is reserved for off-path targets (branch switch) and post-selection resets. This preserves the indexed in-place rewind intent of d59fe05.

**Real behavior proof (in-process harness, real entry points).** The test `proves /status clears and returns across navigation and fork` seeds a session through the production append owner (pre-change stored shape: `compactionQualityDegraded: true`, `compactionCount: 2`), then drives the real SQLite accessor (`rewindSessionToMessage`, `switchSessionBranch`, `forkSessionAtMessage`) and the real /status renderer (`buildStatusMessageParts`). Rendered Compactions line at each step:

```text
/status before:             Compactions: 2 · degraded history (details may be lost)
/status after rewind:        [no Compactions line]
/status after branch switch: Compactions: 0 · degraded history (details may be lost)
/status on clean fork:       [no Compactions line]
/status on degraded fork:    Compactions: 0 · degraded history (details may be lost)
```

**Data-model compatibility.** The harness above loads the exact rows the stable release writes (seeded through the production append owner, untouched by this PR) with the changed code; the 2 → 0 count across navigation is the compatibility evidence.

**Failing-first.** The fork-budget regression test fails on the pre-fix code with `Session history editor/header content exceeds the 8 MiB navigation budget` and passes after. The rewind-scan regression test fails on the pre-fix code (the precheck issued the canonical navigation scan twice) and passes after (no `identity_count` query). Fork-flag assertions fail on base b647c1be (degraded fork: flag undefined instead of true) and pass after.

**Test results (direct vitest, `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=2048`):**

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| SQLite message-cut (infra) | 20/20 (17 existing + 3 new) |
| Memory fork (runtime-config) | 8/8 |
| sessions-rewind + incognito (gateway-methods) | 30/30 |
| status-message (unit-fast-isolated) | 28/28 |

Format clean, oxlint 0 warnings/errors, `git diff --check` clean.
`pnpm tsgo:core` was not run locally (OOM on this machine, peak ~8.4 GiB vs 6.1 GiB cgroup) — CI must run it.

prs.title: fix(google): record the measured context size so Gemini sessions compact at their real occupancy
prs.body:
## Problem

`test/prompt-cache-prefix-stability.google.e2e.test.ts` is red on main (`expected 2 to be 1`). An unrelated chat on a 64,000-token window receives 24 tool results of 8,000 characters each. It compacts twice inside that run (requests 14 and 25), where Anthropic, Bedrock and both OpenAI transports compact once. Every PR that runs this lane needs an override.

The same cause reaches Gemini users: their sessions compact before their context is full.

## Root cause

`packages/ai/src/providers/google-stream.ts` fills `usage` from `usageMetadata` but never sets `usage.contextUsage`. Every other transport records the measured request size there:
- Anthropic: `anthropic-usage.ts`
- OpenAI Responses and Completions: `openai-transport-shared.ts`
- Bedrock: `extensions/amazon-bedrock/stream.runtime.ts`

The pre-request pressure check (`preemptive-compaction.ts`, `resolveProviderContextBoundary`) starts from the last assistant turn's measured `contextUsage` and estimates only what came after it. A Gemini turn has none. So every check re-estimated the entire history locally, with the 1.2 safety margin, and crossed the compaction threshold well before the real occupancy.

## Fix

At the Google stream owner, record `contextUsage` once the terminal chunk reports a prompt count:
- `promptTokens` = `promptTokenCount` (Gemini includes cached content in it) + `toolUsePromptTokenCount`
- `totalTokens` = prompt tokens + candidate tokens + thought tokens

Before the terminal chunk, or with no prompt count, it is `unavailable`, as on the other transports.

The journey had one known break for Google, "the pressure check trims tool results that earlier requests already sent". That trim did not occur on main either: main's only breaks in that chat are compactions. Per the journey's own rule ("a known break that no longer occurs has landed: remove its entry"), the entry is removed, with its now-unused matcher helpers and unit case. The journey is stricter: any trim now fails it.

## Impact

- Gemini (Google Generative AI) users on the embedded runtime, through the Gateway and in one-shot runs: the compaction decision uses the size Google measured, as on every other provider, instead of a padded local re-estimate. Long sessions with large tool results compact later and less often, and keep more detail.
- Status and session usage readers now get Gemini's measured context size, the same as for other providers.

## Evidence

- `packages/ai/src/providers/google-shared.test.ts`: red on main `8b36e346` (2 failed / 35: no `contextUsage`), green on this branch (35/35). Cases cover a measured terminal report with cache and tool-use tokens, sparse usage with no prompt count, and a non-terminal report.
- `test/prompt-cache-prefix-known-breaks.test.ts`: 2/2; test-root typecheck clean.
- Main's CI log (Bun shard) for the journey lists three breaks in the unrelated chat. Two are compactions inside the overflow run: 125 KB at request 14, then 114 KB at request 25. The third is the explicit compaction. None of them is a trim.
- The Google journey itself runs on this PR's CI (a local run was not practical on the shared build host).

prs.title: improve: start SQLite schema inspectors earlier during Gateway startup
prs.body:
Related to #145679

## What Problem This Solves

A Gateway starting with an existing SQLite store waits for a fresh process to load the schema inspector before it can finish database admission.

## User Impact

SQLite-backed Gateway starts can reach the HTTP listener sooner. On an AWS `m7a.2xlarge` with the repository’s `teamBoot` fixture, I ran six interleaved launches per build with eight agents and 10,000 sessions. Each launch received a copy of the same prepared SQLite state.

| From process spawn | Main median / p95 | PR median / p95 | Paired median saving |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| HTTP listener log | 9.06 / 9.10 s | 8.61 / 8.68 s | 421 ms, 6/6 faster |
| First authenticated `sessions.list` | 10.17 / 10.41 s | 9.88 / 10.57 s | 381 ms, 5/6 faster |
| `/readyz` | 11.54 / 11.66 s | 11.04 / 12.34 s | 348 ms, 5/6 faster |

## Why This Change Was Made

The inspector loads code while startup does its existing preparation. The admissible database, live ownership, read transaction, and schema result still come from the existing preflight. Startup joins unused inspectors and skips the early fork when prepared schema facts are available.

## Evidence

- I compared separate runtime builds of `d41719aa71f` and `bf157c3807c` using `scripts/bench-gateway-startup.ts --case teamBoot` on Node 24.19.0. The slower candidate readiness sample retried `sessions.list` while the agent database registry was publishing.
- I started the candidate Gateway on an isolated SQLite schema-41 fixture. It migrated to 42, preserved the sentinel row, and reached readiness. With schema 43, it exited 78 before binding and preserved the database bytes.
- I reran six pairs with Linux cgroup accounting through clean shutdown. Median CPU was 30.96 s on main and 28.30 s on the PR. The p95 values were 32.07 s and 32.70 s. The HTTP listener was faster in all six pairs again.
- Local ClawSweeper reviewed `d41719aa71f..bf157c3807c` and reported no findings.
- 73 focused tests passed across six files. Core typechecking, touched-file lint and formatting also passed.

prs.title: fix(ci): clear stale restart-sentinel exports from the dependency report
prs.body:
Related: #198611, #206700, #206924, #206963

## What Problem This Solves

After #206700 retired the update-report receipt writer, three restart-sentinel exports lost their external production caller. Main already removed the unused exports in #206963. This PR keeps the managed-handoff fixture and the store from maintaining separate copies of the row encoder.

## User Impact

No change to the restart-sentinel row format, lookup behavior, or revision calculation is intended.

## Why This Change Was Made

The keyed reader and revision counter stay private to the store. A separate module owns the payload schema, type and encoder; it does not import the store. The managed-handoff fixture uses that encoder and keeps main’s assertion that the Gateway decodes the published payload. The read-worker test still constructs its own rows independently, as on main.

## Evidence

- [Gateway test type-check on AWS](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_03747d71727831217ccd59aa1d667952): the main base `58ed1818bbbd` passed. The old PR head `9f618874608d` reproduced [TS2724 in check-test-types-core-2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46078274477/job/140771972220). The gateway test now imports the payload type from the codec, with no assertion or runtime change. Both CI type-check stripes and all four tests in that file passed on the tree published at `5b0f058d4d49`.
- [Main Madge control](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_5a27986fc1fafdb3f1b82cd7abe834b8): zero cycles. The [old PR job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/46070400074/job/140746339894) found one cycle between the new row module and the store; [AWS reproduced the failure and verified the fix](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_724fa5db9d10654500874dcba6063af6).
- Before the test-only import fix, the [AWS run on the resolved merge tree](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_5191156c88fee3584ce97e5dbd0a380c) passed the runtime and static cycle checks, Kysely guardrails, the full Knip report, focused tests, and real upgrades from 2026.9.37 and 2026.10.34.

Co-authored with @daniel-lxs.

prs.title: fix(cron): verify recurring job backoff in the live scheduler test
prs.body:
Related: #203106

## What Problem This Solves

The live scheduler test waited for a recurring job to be disabled after its tenth failed run. That cutoff was removed intentionally, so the test timed out before reaching declaration recovery.

## User Impact

No scheduler behavior changes. The live check now fails if the scheduler disables the job, skips backoff, or cannot recover a stopped declaration.

## Why This Change Was Made

A daily interval could pass a backoff check on cadence alone. The fixture now runs every minute and checks that the tenth failure leaves it enabled, without an auto-disable marker, with the next run exactly one hour after the command finished. Redeclaring the still-enabled job preserves its streak and retry time. After an explicit disable, the same declaration re-enables the same job, clears the streak, and is a no-op when repeated. Both scheduled failures must appear in run history.

## Evidence

I ran `pnpm test:live src/gateway/gateway-cron-scheduler.live.test.ts` against a real isolated Gateway on the same CrabBox AWS lease:

- [Main, `8b36e346`](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_8af0fda824bd570e1975af560978e7f9): failed at line 566 with 10 consecutive errors, no auto-disable marker, and a retry nearly 24 hours later.
- [Changed test](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_37e19f0376c25a797e219dafbc81ebc4): 1/1 passed; the case took 84.9 seconds. Formatting and lint passed. The [Gateway test typecheck](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_a541dba90df796e02353ecf5be0eb679) passed separately.

I did not run the full suite or an independent local review. The diff is test-only (+24/-8).

Co-authored with @daniel-lxs.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/task-cron-live-test-stale-cutoff-s60a88ec0)

prs.title: fix(android): retain finalized phrases across native Talk recognition segments
prs.body:
Fixes #195844

## Problem and change

Native Android Talk could discard earlier finalized words when the speech recognizer restarted before the turn's silence timeout. A later partial or final result replaced the separate native transcript string.

Use the existing finalized-segment/live-partial accumulator and transcript merger for native Talk as well as push-to-talk. Silence completion and microphone mute consume that same transcript; the existing turn/capture cleanup clears it. This removes the competing transcript representation and mode-specific merge branch (production +21/-32 lines).

Recognition ownership, callback identity checks, permissions, capture leases, PTT release, and mute draining are unchanged. No configuration or data migration is needed.

## Validation

- **Fresh owner-boundary reproduction:** replayed this PR's exact two-file patch on qualified Android source `4f59076dfe62aeb479bd22084f43a1b1ad70b262`, preserving intervening imports and lifecycle code. With only the tests applied, the committed multi-segment regression and an additional local-only multi-segment mute probe both failed: expected `Send the agenda. Then book the room.`, received `Then book the room.`. Stop/restart isolation passed.
- **Fixed replay:** `TalkModeManagerTest` and `PushToTalkTranscriptMergerTest` passed in both Play and third-party flavors: 131 tests per flavor (130 committed tests plus the local-only mute probe). Coverage includes partial/final continuation, clean subsequent turns, stop, stale callbacks, takeover, PTT release and mute completion. App `ktlintCheck` passed after correcting formatting in that temporary probe. The original failed lint result was retained; production and committed test sources needed no repair.
- **Fresh independent review:** local ClawSweeper reviewed the complete committed range `3a48d6f3ba7735d9bb44b9dc4e795e2487e7396f..d0680c339c08431eb49b72f7b6d9d6d150328f5c`, both changed files, with no actionable findings; patch correct, confidence 0.88. A separate full-owner review also found no defect. The offline reviewer did not ingest the runtime logs above.
- **[Exact PR-head CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42599186471):** Android Play, third-party, ktlint, native i18n and CI gate passed on `d0680c339c08431eb49b72f7b6d9d6d150328f5c`. That retained CI evidence is separate from the fresh current-owner replay.
- **Limit:** these fresh checks use the production Talk owner with Robolectric and an isolated Gateway fixture, not a physical speech engine. The original issue reports earlier device evidence on a different source revision; no fresh device result is claimed here. Temporary proof edits were restored byte-for-byte after execution.

## Contributor credit

This preserves the patch from [the contributor's refreshed source commit](https://github.com/saariuslystoned/openclaw/commit/f84a0e8e2d662e4ebb5e3098324ddd3102c5795f). Verified author: @saariuslystoned (Bobby Bones).
